FunctionInfo.Title: Ackley optimization landscape
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Ackley(real xi1, real xi2, ...)

A multimodal benchmark with a narrow basin at the origin and many shallow surrounding minima.

Definition

Arguments / value: Supply d≥1 real coordinates. The mathematical global minimum is 0 at the all-zero vector.

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

The central basin is surrounded by periodic local structure. Use it to test whether an optimizer can reach the narrow global basin from several starting points, not just whether it decreases the objective once.

Reading the landscape

The two-coordinate landscape has a narrow central basin and repeated shallow basins around it. Coloured curves join equal objective values. The orange line is the y=0 cross-section shown on the right; the marked global minimum is at (0,0).

Worked example

Ackley(0,0)

Result: approximately 0

At the origin the average squared coordinate is zero and the average cosine is one. The two exponential terms cancel 20+e; floating-point arithmetic may leave a tiny residual.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Ai Airy function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Ai(real x)

The Airy solution that decays for large positive .

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x; derivative is with respect to x. These are unscaled values and may overflow/underflow for large positive x.

The Airy equation is a model for a turning point: on one side solutions oscillate, while on the other they grow or decay. This is why Airy functions appear near the boundary between oscillatory and evanescent waves.

Ai is the solution that decays for positive x; Bi grows there. The Prime functions return slopes with respect to x, not squares or derivatives with respect to an order parameter. Choosing the correct solution matters more than merely satisfying the differential equation.

Worked example

Ai(0)

Result: approximately 0.3550280539

The value at the turning point is finite and nonzero; Ai does not mean a function that vanishes at x=0.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Ai negative zero by index
FunctionInfo.Description:
real AiZeros(real x)

Returns the -th negative real zero, ordered outward from the origin, of .

Definition

Arguments / value: The argument x is an INDEX, not a coordinate. Supply a positive integer starting at 1.

Important: The wrapper rounds x to the nearest integer with midpoint ties away from zero; x<0.5 is rejected. Avoid noninteger or out-of-range indices.

The input selects a zero by index; it is not the x coordinate at which Ai or Bi is evaluated. Distinguish zeros of the function from zeros of its derivative, since they impose different boundary conditions.

Example: AiZeros(1) ≈ -2.3381074105

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Bernoulli — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Bernoulli.CDF(real p, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . One success/failure trial: for success and for failure.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: 0≤p≤1; k is 0 or 1.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

A Bernoulli variable records one yes/no outcome. Averaging many independent trials estimates the success probability; adding a fixed number of them gives a binomial count.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Bernoulli.PMF(0.25,1)

Result: 0.25

The mass at one is the success probability, not a density height.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Bernoulli — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool Bernoulli.IsValidParameterSet(real p)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. One success/failure trial: for success and for failure.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: 0≤p≤1; k is 0 or 1.

Important: This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

A Bernoulli variable records one yes/no outcome. Averaging many independent trials estimates the success probability; adding a fixed number of them gives a binomial count.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

FunctionInfo.Title: Bernoulli — Probability mass P(X=k)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Bernoulli.PMF(real p, integer k)

Probability mass . One success/failure trial: for success and for failure.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: 0≤p≤1; k is 0 or 1. Evaluate at integer k in the stated support.

Important: A mass is a point probability between 0 and 1.

A Bernoulli variable records one yes/no outcome. Averaging many independent trials estimates the success probability; adding a fixed number of them gives a binomial count.

Add point masses for disjoint allowed outcomes to obtain their combined probability. Unlike a continuous density, this number already refers to an individual outcome, so no bin width is needed.

FunctionInfo.Title: Bernstein approximation constant
FunctionInfo.Description:
real BernsteinConstantβ

Asymptotic coefficient for the best uniform polynomial approximation to on .

Definition / convention: β=lim(n→∞) n·min(deg p≤n) max(|x|≤1) ||x|−p(x)|.

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0.2801694990238691. Dimensionless.

Important: This is a minimax approximation constant, not a Bernstein-polynomial coefficient. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Evaluating this identifier retrieves its stored numerical approximation; it does not run the defining infinite series, limit or geometric construction. Use the definition to understand the constant and the stored-value line to judge the numerical precision actually available.

Equality in a mathematical identity does not imply bit-for-bit equality after floating-point evaluation. When checking a relation involving this constant, compare an error or residual against an appropriate tolerance instead of demanding exact equality.

The solution regular at the origin for nonnegative integer order.

FunctionInfo.Title: Beta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Beta(real a, real b)

The beta integral; the normalization connecting two gamma factors.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real a>0 and b>0 in this wrapper; symmetric in a and b.

The beta integral balances powers of the distances to the two ends of the unit interval. Interchanging a and b reflects t about one half, so the complete beta function is symmetric.

Dividing the integrand by produces a probability density on . The complete special function is a normalization constant, not the Beta distribution object and not a cumulative probability.

Example: Beta(1,1) = 1

Worked example

Beta(2,3)

Result: approximately 0.0833333333

Γ(2)Γ(3)/Γ(5)=1·2/24=1/12.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Lower incomplete beta
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Beta(real x, real a, real b)

The lower beta integral accumulated up to , without division by the complete beta function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real 0≤x≤1 and a,b>0; out-of-domain values return NaN. The first argument is the integration limit and the other two are shape parameters.

Important: The public order is x,a,b; Meta.Numerics receives Beta(a,b,x). This is an unnormalized area: Beta(0,a,b)=0 and Beta(1,a,b)=Beta(a,b). Use BetaNorm for the corresponding cumulative probability.

Incomplete beta stops the beta integral at x rather than at one. It is an accumulated area, not yet a probability until normalized by the complete beta function.

The first argument sets the upper integration limit; a and b determine the shape of the integrand. At x=0 the area is zero, and at x=1 it equals the complete beta function.

Worked example

Beta(0.5,1,1)

Result: 0.5

With both shapes equal to one the integrand is one, so the area from zero to 0.5 is 0.5.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Beta — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Beta.CDF(real a, real b, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A bounded continuous distribution for proportions on the unit interval.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: Shape parameters a>0 and b>0; 0<x<1. Endpoint limits may be infinite when a or b is below one.

Important: The library has limiting/degenerate cases at zero or infinite shapes. Use strictly positive finite shapes for the ordinary beta density; the short Beta class name collides with the scalar Beta special function in generated TSL. Use MathNet.Numerics.Distributions.Beta.PDF(a,b,x), or the corresponding fully qualified member, to avoid that collision. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The two shapes control behavior near zero and one. Equal shapes make the density symmetric, while shapes below one can concentrate density near the endpoints. A density spike is not a positive point probability at that endpoint.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: MathNet.Numerics.Distributions.Beta.PDF(1,1,0.5) = 1: uniform density on [0,1].

Worked example

MathNet.Numerics.Distributions.Beta.PDF(2,2,0.5)

Result: 1.5

The symmetric density peaks above one. Its area, not its peak height, is the probability. The qualified class name avoids the scalar Beta function name collision in TSL.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Returns a lazy, potentially unending sample sequence. Enumerate only the number of draws you need; it is not a finite materialized array. A bounded continuous distribution for proportions on the unit interval.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: Shape parameters a>0 and b>0; 0<x<1. Endpoint limits may be infinite when a or b is below one. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: The library has limiting/degenerate cases at zero or infinite shapes. Use strictly positive finite shapes for the ordinary beta density; the short Beta class name collides with the scalar Beta special function in generated TSL. Use MathNet.Numerics.Distributions.Beta.PDF(a,b,x), or the corresponding fully qualified member, to avoid that collision. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

The two shapes control behavior near zero and one. Equal shapes make the density symmetric, while shapes below one can concentrate density near the endpoints. A density spike is not a positive point probability at that endpoint.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Worked example

MathNet.Numerics.Distributions.Beta.PDF(2,2,0.5)

Result: 1.5

The symmetric density peaks above one. Its area, not its peak height, is the probability. The qualified class name avoids the scalar Beta function name collision in TSL.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Regularized incomplete beta
FunctionInfo.Description:
real BetaNorm(real x, real a, real b)

The lower beta integral divided by , giving a cumulative probability for positive shape parameters.

Definition / convention: Iₓ(a,b)=Bₓ(a,b)/B(a,b).

Arguments / value: Real 0≤x≤1 and a,b>0; out-of-domain values return NaN. The value is in [0,1], with endpoints zero and one.

Important: The public order is x,a,b; GSL receives gsl_sf_beta_inc(a,b,x). Unlike Beta(x,a,b), this function includes normalization by the complete beta integral.

Normalization turns the incomplete beta area into a cumulative probability for positive shapes. The first argument x is the integration limit; a and b are the shape parameters. For a=b=1 the density is uniform and the result is x.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

BetaNorm(0.5,1,1)

Result: 0.5

With a uniform density on [0,1], half of the total probability lies below 0.5.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Bi Airy function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Bi(real x)

The independent Airy solution that grows for large positive .

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x; derivative is with respect to x. These are unscaled values and may overflow/underflow for large positive x.

The Airy equation is a model for a turning point: on one side solutions oscillate, while on the other they grow or decay. This is why Airy functions appear near the boundary between oscillatory and evanescent waves.

Ai is the solution that decays for positive x; Bi grows there. The Prime functions return slopes with respect to x, not squares or derivatives with respect to an order parameter. Choosing the correct solution matters more than merely satisfying the differential equation.

Example: Bi(0) ≈ 0.6149266274

Worked example

Ai(0)

Result: approximately 0.3550280539

The value at the turning point is finite and nonzero; Ai does not mean a function that vanishes at x=0.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

Returns the -th negative real zero, ordered outward from the origin, of .

FunctionInfo.Title: Binomial — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Binomial.CDF(real p, integer n, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The number of successes among independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability .

Distribution model

Arguments / value: n is a nonnegative integer; 0≤p≤1; integer k ranges from 0 to n.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Use this model for a fixed number of independent trials with the same success chance. When sampling without replacement from a small population, those trials are dependent and the hypergeometric model is more appropriate.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: Binomial.PMF(0.5,2,1) = 0.5.

Worked example

Binomial.PMF(0.5,4,2)

Result: 0.375

Choose the two successful trials in six ways, each pattern having probability 1/16.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. The number of successes among independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability .

Distribution model

Arguments / value: n is a nonnegative integer; 0≤p≤1; integer k ranges from 0 to n.

Important: This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Use this model for a fixed number of independent trials with the same success chance. When sampling without replacement from a small population, those trials are dependent and the hypergeometric model is more appropriate.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

FunctionInfo.Title: Binomial — Probability mass P(X=k)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Binomial.PMF(real p, integer n, integer k)

Probability mass . The number of successes among independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability .

Distribution model

Arguments / value: n is a nonnegative integer; 0≤p≤1; integer k ranges from 0 to n. Evaluate at integer k in the stated support.

Important: A mass is a point probability between 0 and 1.

Use this model for a fixed number of independent trials with the same success chance. When sampling without replacement from a small population, those trials are dependent and the hypergeometric model is more appropriate.

Add point masses for disjoint allowed outcomes to obtain their combined probability. Unlike a continuous density, this number already refers to an individual outcome, so no bin width is needed.

Example: Binomial.PMF(0.5,2,1) = 0.5.

FunctionInfo.Title: Binomial coefficient
FunctionInfo.Description:
real BinomialCoeff(integer n, integer k)

Counts -element subsets of distinct objects when order is irrelevant.

Definition

Arguments / value: Integers 0≤k≤n, representable by the underlying unsigned integer interface; invalid signed bounds return NaN.

Important: The result is floating point rather than an arbitrary-precision integer.

Start with the ordered selections of k objects from n, then divide by the k! ways of ordering each selected group. The result counts groups, not sequences.

The equality C(n,k)=C(n,n−k) follows by exchanging the chosen and unchosen objects. These values grow rapidly, so a floating-point result is not an arbitrary-precision integer count.

Example: BinomialCoeff(5,2) = 10

Worked example

Combinations(5,2)

Result: 10

There are 5·4=20 ordered pairs, but each unordered pair is counted twice.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Bit-vector dot product
FunctionInfo.Description:
integer BitwiseDotProduct(integer x, integer y)

Counts bit positions where both signed 32-bit integer representations contain a one.

Definition / convention: popcount(x AND y)

Arguments / value: Uses all 32 bits, including the sign bit of negative integers.

Important: This returns an integer count, NOT the parity-only dot product over the field with two elements.

The result counts shared set bits over all 32 bit positions. It is not a parity-reduced inner product over a two-element field; negative integers also contribute their sign bit.

Mathematical interpretation

FunctionInfo.Title: Blažys prime continued-fraction constant
FunctionInfo.Description:
real BlazysConstant

A real-number encoding of the prime sequence through a generalized continued fraction.

Definition / convention: B=2+2/(3+3/(5+5/(7+7/(11+…)))).

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 2.566543832171389. Dimensionless.

Important: This is not an independent prime-finding shortcut: the continued fraction already uses the primes. Iterating a finite-precision stored approximation cannot reliably recover arbitrarily many primes. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Evaluating this identifier retrieves its stored numerical approximation; it does not run the defining infinite series, limit or geometric construction. Use the definition to understand the constant and the stored-value line to judge the numerical precision actually available.

Equality in a mathematical identity does not imply bit-for-bit equality after floating-point evaluation. When checking a relation involving this constant, compare an error or residual against an appropriate tolerance instead of demanding exact equality.

Stored numeric value

Reference: oeis.org

FunctionInfo.Title: First Bohachevsky benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Bohachevsky1(real x, real y)

A two-dimensional bowl with periodic local structure.

Standard benchmark definition

Arguments / value: Real x,y. The displayed standard form has minimum 0 at (0,0), but the pinned implementation omits +0.7 and has value -0.7 at that same minimizer. Add 0.7 explicitly when comparing with the standard benchmark.

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

The differently scaled coordinates and oscillations test how an optimizer handles directional curvature. The displayed standard form has its minimum zero at the origin. The pinned Math.NET implementation omits the final +0.7 and returns -0.7 there instead. This vertical shift changes objective values, not the minimizing coordinates; evaluating the function does not search for them.

Reading the landscape

This drawing follows the value returned by Bohachevsky1, whose minimum is -0.7 at the origin. Adding 0.7 produces the standard definition above: every height changes, while the contours and minimizing coordinates keep their shapes and positions.

Worked example

Bohachevsky1(0,0)+0.7

Result: approximately 0

The current implementation returns -0.7 at the origin. Adding the omitted constant recovers the standard benchmark value zero; this is an explicit normalization correction, not the raw function result.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Categorical — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Categorical.CDF(Double[] probabilityMass, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A discrete choice among zero-based category indices, weighted by the supplied nonnegative masses.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: probabilityMass/p is a nonempty array of finite nonnegative weights with positive total; it need not sum to one.

Important: The result is a category INDEX, not the corresponding weight. The order of the array defines the category labels. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

The array positions are the outcome labels. Weights [1,3] mean that label 1 is three times as likely as label 0; they do not mean the possible returned values are 1 and 3.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Categorical.PMF(new double[]{1,3},1)

Result: 0.75

The second category receives weight 3 out of total weight 4. Its index is one.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Categorical — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
integer Categorical.InvCDF(Double[] probabilityMass, real probability)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A discrete choice among zero-based category indices, weighted by the supplied nonnegative masses.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: probabilityMass/p is a nonempty array of finite nonnegative weights with positive total; it need not sum to one. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: The result is a category INDEX, not the corresponding weight. The order of the array defines the category labels. The mathematical lower quantile is the smallest index whose cumulative probability reaches the requested level. Math.NET 5.0 uses binary search and is not guaranteed to return the first equal cumulative weight when zero-mass categories create ties. For example, Categorical.InvCDF(new double[]{1,0,0,1},0.5) returns 1, although the lower quantile is 0. The cumulative-array overload has the same limitation.

The array positions are the outcome labels. Weights [1,3] mean that label 1 is three times as likely as label 0; they do not mean the possible returned values are 1 and 3.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

Worked example

Categorical.PMF(new double[]{1,3},1)

Result: 0.75

The second category receives weight 3 out of total weight 4. Its index is one.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A discrete choice among zero-based category indices, weighted by the supplied nonnegative masses.

Important: The result is a category INDEX, not the corresponding weight. The order of the array defines the category labels. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

The array positions are the outcome labels. Weights [1,3] mean that label 1 is three times as likely as label 0; they do not mean the possible returned values are 1 and 3.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

FunctionInfo.Title: Cauchy (Lorentz) — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Cauchy.CDF(real location, real scale, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A symmetric heavy-tailed distribution with location equal to its median and mode.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real.

Important: The mean and variance do not exist. A finite sample average is not an estimate of a finite theoretical Cauchy mean. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Large outliers are an intrinsic part of this model. Its location is a median, but the population mean and variance are undefined; reporting a finite sample variance does not create finite theoretical moments.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Cauchy.CDF(0,1,0)

Result: 0.5

Symmetry places half the probability below the location; this does not imply that a population mean exists.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Cauchy (Lorentz) — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Cauchy.InvCDF(real location, real scale, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A symmetric heavy-tailed distribution with location equal to its median and mode.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: The mean and variance do not exist. A finite sample average is not an estimate of a finite theoretical Cauchy mean. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Large outliers are an intrinsic part of this model. Its location is a median, but the population mean and variance are undefined; reporting a finite sample variance does not create finite theoretical moments.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

Worked example

Cauchy.CDF(0,1,0)

Result: 0.5

Symmetry places half the probability below the location; this does not imply that a population mean exists.

FunctionInfo.Title: Chi-squared — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ChiSquared.CDF(real freedom, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The sum of squares of independent standard normals for integer degrees of freedom, extended to positive real freedom.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; x≥0. This is Gamma(shape=ν/2, rate=1/2), not a chi variable.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

A sum of squared standardized Gaussian residuals produces this law when the independence and parameter-count assumptions hold. The degrees of freedom describe independent contributions, not a scale to multiply the observed value by.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

ChiSquared.CDF(2,2)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

Two degrees of freedom give an exponential law with rate one half.

FunctionInfo.Title: Chi-squared — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ChiSquared.InvCDF(real freedom, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. The sum of squares of independent standard normals for integer degrees of freedom, extended to positive real freedom.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; x≥0. This is Gamma(shape=ν/2, rate=1/2), not a chi variable. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

A sum of squared standardized Gaussian residuals produces this law when the independence and parameter-count assumptions hold. The degrees of freedom describe independent contributions, not a scale to multiply the observed value by.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

FunctionInfo.Title: Combinations without repetition
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Combinations(integer n, integer k)

Number of unordered selections of distinct objects from objects.

Definition

Arguments / value: Use integers n≥0 and 0≤k≤n.

Important: Delegates to Math.NET combinatorics; floating-point overflow/rounding can occur for large inputs.

Start with the ordered selections of k objects from n, then divide by the k! ways of ordering each selected group. The result counts groups, not sequences.

The equality C(n,k)=C(n,n−k) follows by exchanging the chosen and unchosen objects. These values grow rapidly, so a floating-point result is not an arbitrary-precision integer count.

Worked example

Combinations(5,2)

Result: 10

There are 5·4=20 ordered pairs, but each unordered pair is counted twice.

FunctionInfo.Title: Continuous uniform — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ContinuousUniform.CDF(real lower, real upper, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A constant density on a finite interval; equal-length subintervals have equal probabilities.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: Use finite lower<upper. Samples lie between the bounds; the continuous endpoint values have zero point probability.

Important: The library also accepts equal bounds as a point-mass limit. A continuous PDF is a density and can exceed one on a short interval. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Equal-length pieces of the interval have equal probability. Halving the interval doubles the density height so that the total area remains one; a density above one is therefore perfectly possible.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: ContinuousUniform.PDF(0,2,1) = 0.5.

Worked example

ContinuousUniform.PDF(0,0.5,0.25)

Result: 2

Density two over an interval of length one half integrates to total probability one.

FunctionInfo.Title: Conway–Maxwell–Poisson — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ConwayMaxwellPoisson.CDF(real lambda, real nu, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A count distribution with dispersion controlled relative to a Poisson law.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: lambda=λ>0; nu=ν≥0; k is a nonnegative integer. For ν=0, a normalizable law additionally requires λ<1.

Important: ν=1 reduces to Poisson; ν>1 usually underdisperses and 0<ν<1 overdisperses relative to it. The library parameter validator is not a convergence proof for the normalizing series; avoid the improper ν=0, λ≥1 boundary. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

This model changes the relative weight of larger counts through the factorial term. The ordinary Poisson law is the special case ν=1. A parameter check alone does not establish convergence of its normalizing series.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

The radial coordinate ρ and Coulomb parameter η play different roles. Regular and irregular solutions encode different behavior at the origin; derivative and normalization helpers act on those solutions rather than introducing a new potential.

FunctionInfo.Title: Wigner 3-j symbol
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Coupling3j(real j1, real j2, real j3, real m1, real m2, real m3)

An angular-momentum recoupling coefficient with phase and selection rules fixed by the conventional Wigner/Racah definition.

Arguments / value: Arguments are the actual nonnegative integer or half-integer spin values. Magnetic projections must obey |m|≤j, compatible parity and m₁+m₂+m₃=0.

Important: The integer and real 3-j/6-j overloads use DIFFERENT argument units; explicitly use real literals when supplying actual spins.

Recoupling coefficients are amplitudes with phase conventions, not probabilities by themselves. Integer wrappers can encode twice the physical spin; using 1 where 1/2 was intended changes the state space before any arithmetic takes place.

FunctionInfo.Title: Dawson integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Dawson(real x)

An exponentially scaled integral of , often encountered in Gaussian line-shape calculations.

Definition / convention: D(x)=exp(−x²)∫₀ˣ exp(t²) dt

Arguments / value: Real x. It is odd, D(0)=0, and D(x) is asymptotic to 1/(2x) for large |x|.

The exponential prefactor balances the rapidly growing integral. Compute Dawson directly rather than multiplying two extreme intermediate quantities. Near zero it resembles x; in the tails it decays approximately as 1/(2x).

Mathematical interpretation

FunctionInfo.Title: Normalized Debye integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Debye(integer n, real x)

A thermal integral used in lattice heat-capacity and related statistical-physics models.

Definition / convention: Dₙ(x)=n/xⁿ ∫₀ˣ tⁿ/(exp(t)−1) dt; Dₙ(0)=1 for n>0.

Arguments / value: Use integer n=1,…,6 and x≥0 for the supported normalized functions.

Important: Legacy behavior outside these orders is NOT the same definition: n=0 returns 0, and for other n with x>9 the wrapper returns Γ(n+1)ζ(n+1), omitting n/xⁿ. Do not use that fallback as a normalized higher-order Debye function.

The normalization removes the leading small-x power so the mathematical limit at zero is one. Debye functions appear when summing thermal mode contributions; the order is part of the model, not a derivative count.

Example: Debye(1,0) = 1

FunctionInfo.Title: Centered five-point difference
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Derivative.centeredFivePointMethod(function fx, real x, natural order, real eps)

A finite-difference derivative estimate, recursively extended to higher orders.

Definition / convention: [f(x−2h)−8f(x−h)+8f(x+h)−f(x+2h)]/(12h) for order=1.

Arguments / value: Nonnegative integer order; order zero returns fx(x). Step h=x·eps; when it is zero the wrapper substitutes 1e−25.

Important: eps is a step-size parameter, not a guaranteed result error. Extremely small steps lose subtraction accuracy. Recursive higher-order calls retain the chosen eps at every level, with the relative step recalculated at each evaluation point. Prefer the Math.NET derivative entry when appropriate.

Numerical differentiation estimates local change from nearby function values. A smaller step reduces truncation error only until floating-point subtraction and evaluation noise begin to dominate; the smallest possible step is not generally best.

Higher derivative orders amplify noise and cancellation. Check a known smooth example and compare several step sizes before interpreting fine structure in a derivative of sampled or noisy data.

FunctionInfo.Title: Dirichlet — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool Dirichlet.IsValidParameterSet(Double[] alpha)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A joint distribution over probability vectors, often used as a prior on categorical proportions.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: alpha contains positive finite concentration parameters. The returned array has the same dimension, nonnegative components and sum approximately one.

Important: The ordinary density is on the simplex, not all of Euclidean space. A unit concentration vector gives a uniform simplex distribution; library-accepted degenerate parameters need separate care. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

A draw is a whole vector of proportions that must sum to one. Increasing all concentrations while preserving their ratios concentrates draws around the same mean vector; changing the ratios moves that mean.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Dirichlet — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Double[] Dirichlet.Sample(Random rnd, Double[] alpha)

Returns one random draw. A joint distribution over probability vectors, often used as a prior on categorical proportions.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: alpha contains positive finite concentration parameters. The returned array has the same dimension, nonnegative components and sum approximately one. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: The ordinary density is on the simplex, not all of Euclidean space. A unit concentration vector gives a uniform simplex distribution; library-accepted degenerate parameters need separate care. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

A draw is a whole vector of proportions that must sum to one. Increasing all concentrations while preserving their ratios concentrates draws around the same mean vector; changing the ratios moves that mean.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Arguments / value: Real s; the series converges for s>0, with continuation outside that range.

FunctionInfo.Title: Discrete uniform — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real DiscreteUniform.CDF(integer lower, integer upper, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . An equally likely INTEGER from an inclusive integer interval.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: lower and upper are integers with lower≤upper. Both endpoints belong to the support.

Important: Unlike typical Random.Next bounds, this distribution includes the upper endpoint. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Count the possible integer values before computing a mass. A fair six-sided die has six outcomes, including both 1 and 6; this differs from the exclusive upper bound used by many random-number APIs.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

DiscreteUniform.PMF(1,6,6)

Result: approximately 0.1666666667

Both endpoints count, so a fair die has six equally likely integer outcomes.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Double factorial
FunctionInfo.Description:
real DoubleFactorial(integer n)

Product of positive integers with the same parity as .

Definition / convention: n!!=n·(n−2)·…; 0!!=1 and 1!!=1.

Arguments / value: Intended for nonnegative integers. Negative integer arguments return NaN.

Important: The real-argument overload casts to an integer before evaluation, truncating toward zero; fractional inputs are not a generalized double factorial. GSL defines integer orders above 297 as overflow: the return-value mode yields positive infinity and the error-reporting mode throws. Large orders retain this behavior rather than wrapping to a smaller native unsigned integer.

Take every second integer rather than multiplying all integers up to n. Odd and even orders therefore form separate products; this is not factorial(n) applied twice.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

DoubleFactorial(7)

Result: 105

Multiply 7, 5, 3 and 1.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Ei(real x)

The real principal-value exponential integral, useful in growth, decay and transport problems.

Definition / convention: Ei(x)=PV ∫₋∞ˣ exp(t)/t dt

Arguments / value: Real x≠0. PV specifies the Cauchy principal value across t=0; Ei has a logarithmic singularity there.

The principal-value prescription balances the singular contributions on opposite sides of zero. It is not an ordinary absolutely convergent integral across the pole and should not be reproduced by naive quadrature.

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Entire complementary exponential integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex Ein(complex z)

An entire complex function with the logarithmic singularity removed from .

Definition / convention: Ein(z)=∫₀ᶻ [1−exp(−t)]/t dt = Σₙ₌₁^∞ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹zⁿ/(n·n!)

Arguments / value: Complex z; Ein(0)=0 and the integrand has a removable singularity. This is not Ei(z).

The apparent division by zero is removable: the numerator behaves like t near the origin. This entire function removes the logarithmic complication found in related exponential integrals.

Mathematical interpretation

FunctionInfo.Title: Erlang — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Erlang.CDF(integer shape, real rate, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . An integer-shape gamma distribution: the waiting time for shape events in a Poisson process of the given rate.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape is a positive integer; rate>0; x≥0. Scale is 1/rate.

Important: The ordinary law needs positive shape and rate; the library additionally supports limiting parameter cases. Do not confuse its rate argument with a scale. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

If independent exponential waiting times have the same rate, their sum has an Erlang distribution. The integer shape counts events and the mean waiting time is shape/rate.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Probability density . An integer-shape gamma distribution: the waiting time for shape events in a Poisson process of the given rate.

Distribution model

Important: The ordinary law needs positive shape and rate; the library additionally supports limiting parameter cases. Do not confuse its rate argument with a scale. FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Exponential.CDF(real rate, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The nonnegative, memoryless waiting time to the next event in a constant-rate Poisson process.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: rate>0 and x≥0; rate is inverse mean waiting time, not the mean or scale.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The rate is an event frequency, so the average wait is its reciprocal. The memoryless property says that time already spent waiting does not change the distribution of the remaining wait in this ideal model.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: Exponential.CDF(1,1) = 1−exp(−1).

Worked example

Exponential.CDF(2,0.5)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

At one mean waiting time, 1/rate=0.5, the accumulated probability is 1−e⁻¹.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Exponential.InvCDF(real rate, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. The nonnegative, memoryless waiting time to the next event in a constant-rate Poisson process.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: rate>0 and x≥0; rate is inverse mean waiting time, not the mean or scale. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

The rate is an event frequency, so the average wait is its reciprocal. The memoryless property says that time already spent waiting does not change the distribution of the remaining wait in this ideal model.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

Example: Exponential.CDF(1,1) = 1−exp(−1).

Worked example

Exponential.CDF(2,0.5)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

At one mean waiting time, 1/rate=0.5, the accumulated probability is 1−e⁻¹.

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential — Probability density f(x)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Exponential.PDF(real rate, real x)

Probability density . The nonnegative, memoryless waiting time to the next event in a constant-rate Poisson process.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: rate>0 and x≥0; rate is inverse mean waiting time, not the mean or scale. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

The rate is an event frequency, so the average wait is its reciprocal. The memoryless property says that time already spent waiting does not change the distribution of the remaining wait in this ideal model.

For a short interval of width around , probability is approximately when the density changes slowly there. The approximation improves as the interval shrinks; it is not a probability assigned to the single point .

Example: Exponential.CDF(1,1) = 1−exp(−1).

FunctionInfo.Title: Fisher–Snedecor F — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FisherSnedecor.CDF(real d1, real d2, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The ratio of two independent chi-squared variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: d1>0 and d2>0 are numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, respectively; x≥0.

Important: The mean exists only for d2>2; the variance needs d2>4. Exchanging d1 and d2 describes the reciprocal variable, not the same law. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

This ratio compares two independent estimates of Gaussian variability. The order of the two degrees of freedom matters: reversing numerator and denominator produces a reciprocal random variable.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Fisher–Snedecor F — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FisherSnedecor.InvCDF(real d1, real d2, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. The ratio of two independent chi-squared variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: d1>0 and d2>0 are numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, respectively; x≥0. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

FunctionInfo.Title: Fransén–Robinson constant
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FransénRobinsonConstant

Integral of the reciprocal gamma function over the nonnegative real axis.

Definition / convention: F=∫₀∞ 1/Γ(x) dx.

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 2.8077702420285195. Dimensionless.

Important: The reciprocal gamma function tends to zero at x=0, so the endpoint is interpreted continuously. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Evaluating this identifier retrieves its stored numerical approximation; it does not run the defining infinite series, limit or geometric construction. Use the definition to understand the constant and the stored-value line to judge the numerical precision actually available.

Equality in a mathematical identity does not imply bit-for-bit equality after floating-point evaluation. When checking a relation involving this constant, compare an error or residual against an appropriate tolerance instead of demanding exact equality.

Stored numeric value

Reference: oeis.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Complex Fresnel integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex Fresnel(real x)

Combines the Fresnel cosine and sine integrals into one complex result.

Definition / convention: F(x)=C(x)+iS(x)=∫₀ˣ exp(i·PI·t²/2) dt

Arguments / value: The argument x is real; the result is complex. Both component integrals are zero at the origin.

The real and imaginary parts contain the Fresnel cosine and sine integrals. Keeping both parts is important for interference, where phases combine before taking a magnitude.

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Fresnel cosine integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FresnelC(real x)

The real component of the normalized Fresnel integral, used in diffraction.

Definition / convention: C(x)=∫₀ˣ cos(PI·t²/2) dt

Arguments / value: Real x. The PI/2 factor is part of this convention; C tends to 1/2 as x→+∞.

The oscillations become faster with t because phase is quadratic. This normalized diffraction convention includes π/2; omitting it changes the input scale and limiting normalization.

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Fresnel sine integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FresnelS(real x)

The imaginary component of the normalized Fresnel integral, used in diffraction.

Definition / convention: S(x)=∫₀ˣ sin(PI·t²/2) dt

Arguments / value: Real x. The PI/2 factor is part of this convention; S tends to 1/2 as x→+∞.

This is the sine component of the normalized Fresnel integral. Pair it with C(x) to describe the two coordinates of the Cornu spiral; neither component alone represents the complex amplitude.

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Brent bracketed root finder
FunctionInfo.Description:
real FunctionRoot.BrentMethod(function fx, real a, real b, real errorMax, natural N)

Combines bracketing, interpolation and bisection to find a real zero.

Definition / convention: fx(root) ≈ 0.

Arguments / value: errorMax>0 is the requested solver accuracy; N>0 limits iterations (default 10,000).

Important: Use a continuous fx and a<b with opposite endpoint signs. Returns NaN when TryFindRoot fails. Repeated roots, discontinuities and nonfinite evaluations may defeat convergence.

A sign-changing bracket for a continuous function guarantees at least one root, but not uniqueness. A pole can also change sign, so continuity across the bracket is essential.

Verify both the reported location and its residual f(x*). A small residual can correspond to a large location error near a flat root; a narrow interval alone can also be misleading near a discontinuity.

Target equation

FunctionInfo.Title: Newtonian gravitational constant — short name
FunctionInfo.Description:
real G

Sets the strength of Newtonian gravitational attraction.

Definition / convention: F=G·m₁·m₂/r².

Arguments / value: Unit: m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻². Stored application value: 6.673848E-11.

Important: The short name G and NewtonianConstantOfGravitation have slightly different stored values. G is experimentally determined, not an SI defining constant. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

The symbol in a physical equation denotes a quantity with units; this identifier evaluates to a plain number. Supply the other quantities in the compatible units shown in this entry, because the expression engine does not attach dimensional units or convert them automatically.

FunctionInfo.Title: One-dimensional Gabor function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Gabor(real x, real mean, real amplitude, real position, real width, real phase, real frequency)

A localized sinusoidal signal with a Gaussian envelope and an additive mean.

Definition / convention: Gaussian-windowed cosine with the supplied amplitude, position, width, phase and frequency.

Arguments / value: x is the evaluation coordinate; mean is the offset, position the envelope center, width its positive scale, amplitude its height. Frequency and phase follow Accord’s Function1D convention.

Important: This returns a real scalar. It is distinct from the wavelength/rotation-based complex two-dimensional overload.

A Gabor model localizes an oscillation inside a Gaussian envelope. Width controls spatial localization, while carrier frequency controls oscillation. This displayed one-dimensional model is an interpretation, not a replacement for the exact phase, rotation, offset and scale conventions stated for this overload.

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: accord-framework.net

FunctionInfo.Title: Two-dimensional complex Gabor kernel
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex Gabor(complex z, real λ, real θ, real ψ, real σ, real γ)

A rotated anisotropic Gaussian envelope multiplied by a complex sinusoid.

Definition / convention: exp[−(x′²+γ²y′²)/(2σ²)]·exp[i(2PI·x′/λ+ψ)]

Arguments / value: x′=xcosθ+ysinθ, y′=−xsinθ+ycosθ; θ,ψ are radians, λ is wavelength, σ>0 the envelope width and γ the aspect ratio.

Important: This wrapper takes x=Re(z), y=Im(z) but casts both to integers before calling Accord. Noninteger coordinates are truncated, not sampled continuously.

A Gabor model localizes an oscillation inside a Gaussian envelope. Width controls spatial localization, while carrier frequency controls oscillation. FunctionInfo.Title: Gamma distribution — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Gamma.CDF(real shape, real rate, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A nonnegative waiting-time/scale model with a positive shape parameter, extending Erlang to noninteger shapes.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape>0, rate>0, x≥0; the scale is 1/rate.

Important: This class uses SHAPE/RATE for its ordinary static functions. Library limiting cases at zero/infinite parameters are not the ordinary finite positive-parameter density. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The shape changes the curve while the rate sets its time or length scale. Doubling the rate halves the mean at fixed shape. The shape-one case is exponential; a positive integer shape is Erlang.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Gamma.PDF(1,2,0.5)

Result: approximately 0.7357588823

Shape one reduces gamma to the exponential density with rate two.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Geometric — trials until success — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Geometric.CDF(real p, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The number of Bernoulli trials up to and INCLUDING the first success.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: Use 0<p≤1 for a proper finite waiting-time law. This implementation never samples zero.

Important: This is NOT the alternative failures-before-success convention on 0,1,… . The parameter validator accepts p=0, but that boundary has no finite first-success time. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Count the successful trial itself. With success chance one half, the probability of success on trial one is one half, and success on trial two has probability one quarter. This is a count, not a continuous waiting time.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: Geometric.PMF(0.5,1) = 0.5; the smallest possible sample is 1.

Worked example

Geometric.PMF(0.5,2)

Result: 0.25

One failure followed by one success has probability (1−0.5)·0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Physicists’ Hermite polynomial
FunctionInfo.Description:
real HermiteH(integer n, real x)

A Gaussian-weight orthogonal polynomial; the two common conventions have different scaling.

Definition / convention: Hₙ(x)=(−1)ⁿ exp(x²)dⁿexp(−x²)/dxⁿ

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0; real x.

Important: Hₙ(x)=2^(n/2)Heₙ(sqrt(2)x). H₁(x)=2x whereas He₁(x)=x.

Degree, order and evaluation coordinate are separate inputs. Changing a degree chooses another member of the family, not another point on the same curve. The normalization and weighting convention determine how coefficients from different references can be compared.

Example: HermiteH(2,0) = -2

FunctionInfo.Title: Himmelblau benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Himmelblau(real x, real y)

A two-dimensional polynomial with four equal global minima.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x,y; (3,2) is one global minimizer, with value 0.

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

There are multiple equally good global minimizers. Different starting points can legitimately converge to different answers, so compare objective values and residual conditions rather than demanding one particular coordinate pair.

Reading the landscape

Four separate basins attain the same global value zero; all four minimizing points are marked. The y=2 slice passes through (3,2) but misses the other three minima. A one-dimensional slice alone cannot establish the number of minima of a surface.

Worked example

Himmelblau(3,2)

Result: 0

Both squared terms vanish: 9+2−11=0 and 3+4−7=0.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Hurwitz zeta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real HurwitzZeta(real x, real q)

Shifts the reciprocal-power series away from the positive integers.

Definition / convention: ζ(s,q)=Σₙ₌₀^∞ (n+q)^(−s)

Arguments / value: The argument named x is the exponent s. This real GSL interface requires s>1 and q>0; it is not the full analytic continuation.

The shift q moves the starting point of the reciprocal-power sum. q=1 recovers Riemann zeta in the convergent half-plane; it is not a second exponent.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

HurwitzZeta(2,1)

Result: approximately 1.6449340668

At shift one the sum is 1+1/4+1/9+⋯=π²/6.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Normalized hydrogenic radial wavefunction
FunctionInfo.Description:
real HydrogenicR(integer n, integer l, real Z, real r)

The radial part of a bound-state wavefunction in a point-nucleus Coulomb potential.

Definition / convention: Rₙₗ(r)=2Z^(3/2)/n² · sqrt[(n−l−1)!/(n+l)!] · (2Zr/n)ˡ exp(−Zr/n) Lₙ₋ₗ₋₁^(2l+1)(2Zr/n)

Arguments / value: Integers n≥1, 0≤l<n, nuclear charge Z>0, radius r≥0 in atomic units. The full orbital is Rₙₗ(r)Yₗᵐ(θ,φ).

Important: Radial normalization is ∫₀^∞ |R|²r²dr=1, not ∫|R|²dr=1.

The radial wavefunction must be combined with a spherical harmonic for the complete orbital. The factor r² in the radial volume element matters: integrating |R|² without it tests a different normalization.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

HydrogenicR(1,0,1,0)

Result: 2

At the origin the hydrogen 1s radial factor is two in the atomic-unit convention.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Hypergeometric — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Hypergeometric.CDF(integer population, integer success, integer draws, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The number of successes in draws without replacement from a finite population.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: population, success and draws are integers; 0≤success≤population and 0≤draws≤population. Support: max(0,draws−population+success)≤k≤min(draws,success).

Important: Sampling is without replacement, unlike the independent-trial Binomial model. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Each draw changes the remaining population. That dependence distinguishes sampling without replacement from a binomial experiment and constrains which counts are actually possible.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Each draw changes the remaining population. That dependence distinguishes sampling without replacement from a binomial experiment and constrains which counts are actually possible.

FunctionInfo.Title: Hypergeometric — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
integer Hypergeometric.Sample(integer population, integer success, integer draws)

Returns one random draw. The number of successes in draws without replacement from a finite population.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: population, success and draws are integers; 0≤success≤population and 0≤draws≤population. Support: max(0,draws−population+success)≤k≤min(draws,success). Uses the library’s default random source; no explicit seed is accepted by this overload.

Important: Sampling is without replacement, unlike the independent-trial Binomial model. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

Each draw changes the remaining population. That dependence distinguishes sampling without replacement from a binomial experiment and constrains which counts are actually possible.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

FunctionInfo.Title: Confluent hypergeometric limit function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Hypergeometric0F1(real c, real x)

A hypergeometric function closely related to Bessel functions.

Definition / convention: ₀F₁(;c;x)=Σₖ₌₀^∞ xᵏ/[(c)ₖ k!]

Arguments / value: Real c,x; c must not be zero or a negative integer for the ordinary definition.

Important: The empty numerator parameter list is intentional. The Pochhammer symbol denotes a rising factorial.

The parameters control the differential equation and its normalization, while x is the evaluation coordinate. A terminating series, a convergent series and an asymptotic expansion require different interpretations. The representation below is not permission to sum an infinite series outside its domain.

Example: Hypergeometric0F1(1,0) = 1

FunctionInfo.Title: Double-exponential quadrature

real Integral.simpsonMethod(function fx, real a, real b, real N)

Integrates piecewise quadratic interpolation on pairs of equal-width panels.

Definition / convention: h/3·[f(a)+4f(a+h)+2f(a+2h)+…+4f(b−h)+f(b)].

Arguments / value: fx is a real-valued callable. Supply integral N>0 and finite bounds a,b in either order.

These are numerical estimates, not symbolic antiderivatives or certified error bounds.

Simpson’s rule combines samples with alternating weights four and two. An even subinterval count is required. Smoothness is important: a discontinuity or unresolved narrow peak can defeat a seemingly dense grid.

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse gamma — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real InverseGamma.CDF(real shape, real scale, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A positive distribution obtained by inverting a gamma variable, commonly used for variance modeling.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape>0 and scale>0. Here scale is the β in exp(−β/x), not a gamma rate argument to be inverted again.

Important: E[X]=scale/(shape−1) exists only for shape>1; finite variance requires shape>2. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Reciprocating a gamma variable reverses small and large values. The resulting upper tail can be heavy enough that its mean or variance does not exist even though sampling and the density remain defined.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse Wishart — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool InverseWishart.IsValidParameterSet(real degreesOfFreedom, Matrix scale)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A distribution on symmetric positive-definite matrices, often used as a covariance prior.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: scale=Ψ is a real d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix; degreesOfFreedom=ν>d−1 for a proper nonsingular law.

Important: The scale is Ψ, not the covariance mean. E[X]=Ψ/(ν−d−1) only when ν>d+1. Validation checks do not replace a positive-definite factorization. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

A sample is a covariance-shaped positive-definite matrix. The matrix scale is not automatically its mean; degrees of freedom control concentration and whether the mean exists.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse Wishart — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Matrix InverseWishart.Sample(Random rnd, real degreesOfFreedom, Matrix scale)

Returns one random draw. A distribution on symmetric positive-definite matrices, often used as a covariance prior.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: scale=Ψ is a real d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix; degreesOfFreedom=ν>d−1 for a proper nonsingular law. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: The scale is Ψ, not the covariance mean. E[X]=Ψ/(ν−d−1) only when ν>d+1. Validation checks do not replace a positive-definite factorization. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

A sample is a covariance-shaped positive-definite matrix. The matrix scale is not automatically its mean; degrees of freedom control concentration and whether the mean exists.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Jacobi elliptic cn
FunctionInfo.Description:
real JacobiEllipticCn(real u, real m)

An elliptic analogue of a trigonometric function, parameterized by .

Definition / convention: cn(u|m)=cos(am(u|m))

Arguments / value: Real u and −1≤m≤1 in this wrapper. Here m is the PARAMETER k², unlike the modulus argument of EllipticK/E/F.

Important: Identities: sn²+cn²=1 and dn²+m·sn²=1. At m=0, sn=sin, cn=cos and dn=1.

These generalize trigonometric functions: at parameter m=0, sn and cn reduce to sin and cos and dn becomes one. Here m is the parameter, while Legendre-form elliptic-integral routines use the modulus k; m=k².

Family identities

FunctionInfo.Title: Kronecker tensor product
FunctionInfo.Description:
Matrix KroneckerProduct<T>(Matrix mactrices1, Matrix mactrices2, ...)

Forms a block matrix by replacing each entry of the left operand with that entry times the right operand.

Definition / convention: (A⊗B) block (i,j)=AᵢⱼB.

Arguments / value: Nonempty inputs for indexed left-fold implementations; elementwise operations require equal dimensions.

Important: At least one compatible matrix; folds left to right. Matrix dimensions multiply, so memory grows quickly.

Each entry of A scales a whole copy of B. Dimensions multiply rather than add, so tensor-product constructions can become large even when the factors are modest.

Mathematical interpretation

Combines independent linear operators on a tensor-product space.

Arguments / value: Nonempty inputs for indexed left-fold implementations; elementwise operations require equal dimensions.

Important: Use square matrices for the standard definition; folds left to right. This is not the block-diagonal direct sum.

A Kronecker sum combines operators acting on independent factors of a tensor-product space. It is not the block-diagonal direct sum despite the overlapping mathematical notation.

FunctionInfo.Title: Laplace (double exponential) — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Laplace.CDF(real location, real scale, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The sharp peak and exponential tails distinguish this model from a Gaussian. Its scale is the mean absolute deviation from its location, while its standard deviation is √2 times that scale.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Laplace.CDF(0,1,0)

Result: 0.5

Half the probability lies on each side of the location.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

The sharp peak and exponential tails distinguish this model from a Gaussian. Its scale is the mean absolute deviation from its location, while its standard deviation is √2 times that scale.

Probability density . A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

The sharp peak and exponential tails distinguish this model from a Gaussian. Its scale is the mean absolute deviation from its location, while its standard deviation is √2 times that scale.

FunctionInfo.Title: Laplace (double exponential) — One random draw

real Laplace.Sample(real location, real scale)

Returns one random draw. A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation. Uses the library’s default random source; no explicit seed is accepted by this overload.

Important: Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

The sharp peak and exponential tails distinguish this model from a Gaussian. Its scale is the mean absolute deviation from its location, while its standard deviation is √2 times that scale.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

The sharp peak and exponential tails distinguish this model from a Gaussian. Its scale is the mean absolute deviation from its location, while its standard deviation is √2 times that scale.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Worked example

Laplace.CDF(0,1,0)

Result: 0.5

Half the probability lies on each side of the location.

FunctionInfo.Title: Lognormal — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real LogNormal.CDF(real mu, real sigma, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A positive variable whose natural logarithm is normally distributed.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: mu is the mean of ln X; sigma>0 is the STANDARD DEVIATION of ln X; x>0.

Important: mu and sigma are not the mean and standard deviation of X. E[X]=exp(mu+sigma²/2); sigma=0 is a degenerate limit supported by some library paths. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Multiplicative effects become additive after taking logarithms. The median is exp(mu), whereas the mean is exp(mu+sigma²/2); using mu as the mean of the original positive observations is a parameterization error.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

LogNormal.CDF(0,1,1)

Result: 0.5

The logarithm of one is zero, the center of the associated normal distribution; one is the lognormal median.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Multiplicative effects become additive after taking logarithms. The median is exp(mu), whereas the mean is exp(mu+sigma²/2); using mu as the mean of the original positive observations is a parameterization error.

Parameter estimation answers which parameters summarize the observations under this model. It does not establish that the model fits the data; inspect residuals, tail behavior and domain assumptions separately.

Important: mu and sigma are not the mean and standard deviation of X. E[X]=exp(mu+sigma²/2); sigma=0 is a degenerate limit supported by some library paths. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Multiplicative effects become additive after taking logarithms. The median is exp(mu), whereas the mean is exp(mu+sigma²/2); using mu as the mean of the original positive observations is a parameterization error.
