FunctionInfo.Title: Logistic sigmoid
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Logistic(real x)

Maps a real log-odds value to a probability.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x; mathematical values lie in (0,1), with floating-point saturation at extremes. Logistic(0)=0.5.

Logistic turns a log-odds value into a probability. Zero log-odds means equal odds and therefore probability one half; positive inputs favor success.

An output near zero or one can be extremely sensitive when converted back to log-odds. Finite precision may round to an endpoint, so do not assume that applying Logit after saturation recovers the original input.

Worked example

Logistic(0)

Result: 0.5

Equal odds correspond to a probability of one half.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Log-odds transform
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Logit(real x)

The inverse of the logistic sigmoid on probabilities strictly between zero and one.

Definition

Arguments / value: 0≤p≤1 in this wrapper; endpoints give −∞ and +∞. Outside the interval returns NaN.

Odds compare the probability of success with the probability of failure. Logit takes their natural logarithm, mapping probabilities strictly between zero and one to the real line.

The endpoint probabilities correspond to infinite log-odds. A small numerical change close to an endpoint produces a much larger change in logit than the same change near one half.

Worked example

Logit(0.5)

Result: 0

The odds are 0.5/0.5=1 and ln(1)=0.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Matrix normal — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool MatrixNormal.IsValidParameterSet(Matrix m, Matrix v, Matrix k)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A Gaussian distribution over matrices with separable row and column covariance.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: m is the d×p mean matrix; v is d×d row covariance; k is p×p column covariance. Covariance matrices must be symmetric positive definite.

Important: Matrix shapes are part of the contract; m is a matrix of means, not a scalar dimension. The covariance of vectorized samples is a Kronecker product, not v+k. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Row and column covariance are separate factors of a larger covariance on vectorized entries. Their dimensions must match the mean matrix. The formula uses column stacking, so transposing a matrix also changes the covariance interpretation.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Matrix normal — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Matrix MatrixNormal.Sample(Random rnd, Matrix m, Matrix v, Matrix k)

Returns one random draw. A Gaussian distribution over matrices with separable row and column covariance.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: m is the d×p mean matrix; v is d×d row covariance; k is p×p column covariance. Covariance matrices must be symmetric positive definite. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: Matrix shapes are part of the contract; m is a matrix of means, not a scalar dimension. The covariance of vectorized samples is a Kronecker product, not v+k. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 sampling does not implement the stated column-covariance convention. It builds v⊗k⁻¹ and unpacks the draw by columns, instead of using k⊗v. In the 1×1 case with m=0, v=1 and k=4, the actual sample variance is 1/4, not the intended 4. Do not use this sampler as if k were the advertised column covariance; the formula above describes the mathematical model, not this implementation defect.

Row and column covariance are separate factors of a larger covariance on vectorized entries. Their dimensions must match the mean matrix. The formula uses column stacking, so transposing a matrix also changes the covariance interpretation.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Matyas benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Matyas(real x, real y)

A shallow quadratic valley used to test numerical minimization.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x,y; minimum 0 at (0,0).

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

The mixed term rotates and flattens the quadratic valley. It gives a simple example in which coordinate directions are not the principal curvature directions.

Reading the landscape

The long contour ellipses follow the diagonal y=x: changing both coordinates together moves along the shallow valley. Along that orange diagonal the function reduces to 0.04x². Perpendicular to it, along y=-x, the curvature is much stronger.

Worked example

Matyas(0,0)

Result: 0

All quadratic contributions vanish at the origin.

FunctionInfo.Title: Multinomial — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool Multinomial.IsValidParameterSet(IEnumerable`1 p, integer n)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. The vector of category counts from independent categorical trials.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: n is a nonnegative integer; p is a nonempty nonnegative weight array with positive total, normalized internally. The returned integer counts sum to n.

Important: One draw returns the whole count vector, not a single category index. Use Categorical for one category index. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Each experiment returns all category counts. Those counts are dependent because their sum is fixed; increasing one count leaves fewer observations for the others.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Multinomial — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Int32[] Multinomial.Sample(Random rnd, Double[] p, integer n)

Returns one random draw. The vector of category counts from independent categorical trials.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: n is a nonnegative integer; p is a nonempty nonnegative weight array with positive total, normalized internally. The returned integer counts sum to n. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: One draw returns the whole count vector, not a single category index. Use Categorical for one category index. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

Each experiment returns all category counts. Those counts are dependent because their sum is fixed; increasing one count leaves fewer observations for the others.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

FunctionInfo.Title: Negative binomial — failures — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real NegativeBinomial.CDF(real r, real p, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The number of failures before successes; the gamma-function extension also permits positive real .

Distribution model

Arguments / value: r>0, 0<p≤1 for the ordinary law; k is a nonnegative integer. p is the success probability.

Important: E[X]=r(1−p)/p. This counts failures, unlike this library’s Geometric class, which counts trials including the first success. Boundary r=0 or p=0 needs separate limiting interpretation. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Here the variable counts failures, not the total number of trials. For integer r, adding r converts the failure count into a trials-until-r-successes count. The real-shape extension keeps the probability model but not that literal counting story.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

NegativeBinomial.PMF(1,0.5,0)

Result: 0.5

Zero failures before the first success means the first trial succeeds.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Normal (Gaussian) — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Normal.CDF(real mean, real stddev, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A symmetric bell-shaped distribution about its mean. The width is the standard deviation, not the variance.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: mean=μ is real; stddev=σ>0; x is real.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Use a Gaussian model for fluctuations around a center when symmetric light tails are appropriate. A change of units rescales both the mean and standard deviation; it does not turn a standard deviation into a variance.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: Normal.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5; Normal.InvCDF(0,1,0.5) = 0.

Density and accumulated probability

Standard-normal example with μ=0 and σ=1. The shaded left-tail area for X≤1 has probability approximately 0.8413; the orange marker has density f(1)≈0.2420, a height rather than a probability. The drawing shows x from -4 to 4; both tails continue beyond the plotted range, and the stated probability includes the entire left tail.

Worked example

Normal.CDF(0,1,1)-Normal.CDF(0,1,-1)

Result: approximately 0.6826894921

Subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper one to find the probability of lying within one standard deviation.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Use a Gaussian model for fluctuations around a center when symmetric light tails are appropriate. A change of units rescales both the mean and standard deviation; it does not turn a standard deviation into a variance.

Parameter estimation answers which parameters summarize the observations under this model. It does not establish that the model fits the data; inspect residuals, tail behavior and domain assumptions separately.

FunctionInfo.Title: Normal (Gaussian) — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Normal.InvCDF(real mean, real stddev, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A symmetric bell-shaped distribution about its mean. The width is the standard deviation, not the variance.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: mean=μ is real; stddev=σ>0; x is real. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Use a Gaussian model for fluctuations around a center when symmetric light tails are appropriate. A change of units rescales both the mean and standard deviation; it does not turn a standard deviation into a variance.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

Example: Normal.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5; Normal.InvCDF(0,1,0.5) = 0.

Worked example

Normal.CDF(0,1,1)-Normal.CDF(0,1,-1)

Result: approximately 0.6826894921

Subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper one to find the probability of lying within one standard deviation.

FunctionInfo.Title: Pareto — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Pareto.CDF(real scale, real shape, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A heavy-tailed positive distribution with a hard lower cutoff.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Above a minimum size, the tail decays by a power rather than an exponential. Shape controls how severe extreme observations are and whether population moments exist.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Pareto.CDF(1,2,2)

Result: 0.75

The remaining tail above two is (1/2)²=1/4, leaving cumulative probability 3/4.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Above a minimum size, the tail decays by a power rather than an exponential. Shape controls how severe extreme observations are and whether population moments exist.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

FunctionInfo.Title: Poisson — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Poisson.CDF(real lambda, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A count model for independent events in a fixed exposure with a constant average rate.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: lambda=λ>0 is the expected count in the exposure; k is a nonnegative integer.

Important: Specify the exposure separately in your model: λ is a count mean, not necessarily a rate per second. λ=0 has a mathematical point-mass limit but some library entry points require λ>0. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

The parameter is the expected count during the chosen observation interval. Scaling the interval scales that expected count under a constant-rate model. Events must be sufficiently independent for this interpretation.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Example: Poisson.PMF(1,0) = exp(−1).

Worked example

Poisson.PMF(2,0)

Result: approximately 0.1353352832

With expected count two, the probability of no events is e⁻².

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Important: Specify the exposure separately in your model: λ is a count mean, not necessarily a rate per second. λ=0 has a mathematical point-mass limit but some library entry points require λ>0. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

The parameter is the expected count during the chosen observation interval. Scaling the interval scales that expected count under a constant-rate model. Events must be sufficiently independent for this interpretation.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Worked example

Poisson.PMF(2,0)

Result: approximately 0.1353352832

With expected count two, the probability of no events is e⁻².

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Polylogarithm of integer order
FunctionInfo.Description:
real PolyLog(integer n, real x)

A weighted power series continued beyond its disk of convergence.

Definition / convention: Liₙ(x)=Σₖ₌₁^∞ xᵏ/kⁿ for |x|<1.

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0 and real x≤1 in this wrapper; endpoints can diverge for low n.

The order changes the reciprocal-power weighting of the series. Order one connects to −ln(1−z), and order two is the dilogarithm. Do not sum the defining series outside its convergence region as an implementation recipe.

Example: PolyLog(2,1) ≈ PI*PI/6

FunctionInfo.Title: Rastrigin optimization landscape
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Rastrigin(real xi1, real xi2, ...)

A quadratic bowl modulated by a cosine in every coordinate; a test of escaping local minima.

Definition

Arguments / value: Supply d≥1 real coordinates; the global minimum is 0 at the origin.

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

Cosine modulation creates many local minima inside a larger quadratic bowl. A local descent method can stop away from the global minimum even though the function is smooth.

Reading the landscape

The repeated contour islands are local basins inside the larger quadratic bowl. The y=0 slice shows the periodic barriers between them. Only the marked origin attains the global value zero; the nearby basins remain higher.

Worked example

Rastrigin(1,2)

Result: 5

At integer coordinates both cosines equal one. The cosine contributions cancel 10d, leaving 1²+2²=5, above the global value zero.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Rayleigh — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Rayleigh.CDF(real scale, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . The length of a two-dimensional vector of independent zero-mean normal components with equal standard deviation.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the standard deviation of EACH Gaussian component, not the mean radius.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The magnitude of two independent zero-mean Gaussian coordinates with equal standard deviation has this law. It often models a nonnegative amplitude rather than either signed coordinate.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Rayleigh.CDF(1,1)

Result: approximately 0.3934693403

At x equal to the scale, the CDF is 1−e⁻¹ᐟ².

FunctionInfo.Title: Rayleigh — Inverse CDF (quantile)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. The length of a two-dimensional vector of independent zero-mean normal components with equal standard deviation.

Important: Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

The magnitude of two independent zero-mean Gaussian coordinates with equal standard deviation has this law. It often models a nonnegative amplitude rather than either signed coordinate.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

FunctionInfo.Title: Riccati-labelled Bessel combination
FunctionInfo.Description:
real RiccatiBesselC(integer n, real x)

The application’s radial Bessel combination, with its sign and cylindrical/spherical convention made explicit.

Definition / convention: −x·yₙ(x)

Arguments / value: Integer n; use x>0 for irregular/Hankel forms. Singular limits at zero should not be inferred from multiplication by x.

Important: jₙ and yₙ are spherical Bessel functions. C/χ uses a minus sign; some references use the opposite sign.

Bessel functions describe radial modes in cylindrical geometry. Spherical and Riccati variants rescale related half-integer solutions; Hankel functions combine independent solutions into complex waves. Use the specific function and its stated normalization, rather than treating all family names as aliases.

Underlying cylindrical equation

FunctionInfo.Title: Riccati–Hankel function of the second kind
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex RiccatiBesselζ(integer n, real x)

A spherical Hankel wave multiplied by its radial argument, with the same normalization as the real Riccati–Bessel functions S and C.

Definition / convention: ζₙ(x)=x·hₙ⁽²⁾(x)=Sₙ(x)+iCₙ(x)

Arguments / value: Integer n and real x>0. Nonpositive arguments return NaN; the finite order-zero limit at x=0 is not evaluated by this wrapper.

Important: Here Sₙ=x·jₙ and Cₙ=−x·yₙ use spherical Bessel functions. The first and second kinds are complex conjugates on the positive real axis; the outgoing/incoming interpretation also depends on the time convention. For 0<x≤1e−8, the implementation uses scaled radial values to avoid overflowing an intermediate spherical function when the final components remain representable.

Multiplying a spherical Hankel function by its radial argument removes the first-derivative term from the spherical wave equation. These two Riccati–Hankel functions solve the resulting radial equation, with the S and C signs given in their definitions.

Example: RiccatiBesselζ(0,0.5) ≈ 0.4794255386 + 0.8775825619i

Riccati–Bessel equation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Riemann zeta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real RiemannZeta(real x)

Analytic continuation of the sum of reciprocal powers of positive integers.

Definition

Arguments / value: A simple pole occurs at s=1; trivial zeros occur at negative even integers. Complex input uses the meromorphic continuation.

Zeta adds reciprocal powers of the positive integers. The displayed series converges only to the right of Re(s)=1; values elsewhere require analytic continuation rather than summing the same series.

The pole at one is not an ordinary large finite value. At even positive integers there are exact formulas involving powers of π that make useful checks of the numerical implementation.

Worked example

RiemannZeta(2)

Result: approximately 1.6449340668

The reciprocal-square series sums to π²/6.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Normalized hydrogenic radial wavefunction
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Rnl(integer n, integer l, real Z, real r)

The radial part of a bound-state wavefunction in a point-nucleus Coulomb potential.

Definition / convention: Rₙₗ(r)=2Z^(3/2)/n² · sqrt[(n−l−1)!/(n+l)!] · (2Zr/n)ˡ exp(−Zr/n) Lₙ₋ₗ₋₁^(2l+1)(2Zr/n)

Arguments / value: Integers n≥1, 0≤l<n, nuclear charge Z>0, radius r≥0 in atomic units. The full orbital is Rₙₗ(r)Yₗᵐ(θ,φ).

Important: Alias of HydrogenicR with the same convention. Radial normalization is ∫₀^∞ |R|²r²dr=1, not ∫|R|²dr=1.

The radial wavefunction must be combined with a spherical harmonic for the complete orbital. The factor r² in the radial volume element matters: integrating |R|² without it tests a different normalization.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

HydrogenicR(1,0,1,0)

Result: 2

At the origin the hydrogen 1s radial factor is two in the atomic-unit convention.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Rosenbrock valley
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Rosenbrock(real x, real y)

A benchmark whose curved narrow valley makes numerical minimization difficult.

Definition

Arguments / value: Two or more real coordinates. The two-argument overload uses d=2. The global minimum is 0 when all coordinates are 1.

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

The minimum lies in a narrow curved valley. Finding the valley is easier than progressing along it; a small gradient component in one coordinate does not establish convergence in all coordinates.

Reading the landscape

The orange path follows the curved valley y=x², rather than a straight cross-section. On this path the large squared penalty vanishes and only (1-x)² remains, reaching zero at the marked point (1,1). The close contour spacing across the valley shows why movement across it is costly.

Worked example

Rosenbrock(1,1)

Result: 0

Both terms of the two-dimensional expression vanish at one.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Stable — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Stable.CDF(real alpha, real beta, real scale, real location, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A heavy-tail family closed under sums up to location/scale changes; alpha controls the stability index and beta skewness.

Definition / convention: At alpha=2: Normal(location, stddev=sqrt(2)·scale). At alpha=1,beta=0: Cauchy(location,scale).

Arguments / value: 0<alpha≤2, −1≤beta≤1, scale>0; location is real.

Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 implements this evaluation only for alpha=2 (Gaussian), alpha=1 with beta=0 (Cauchy), or alpha=0.5 with beta=1 (Lévy). Other stable parameters throw NotSupportedException even though sampling and IsValidParameterSet accept them. For the Lévy branch, use x>location for ordinary evaluation. At x=location, PDF and PDFLn return NaN instead of their mathematical limits 0 and −∞; CDF returns 0. Below location, PDF/PDFLn throw and CDF returns NaN, although the mathematical density and CDF are zero there.

Stable laws are characterized most generally through a characteristic function, not an elementary density formula. The α, β, scale and location conventions must match the implementation, especially at α=1; sampling support does not imply every PDF/CDF has a closed form.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: 0<alpha≤2, −1≤beta≤1, scale>0; location is real. Uses the library’s default random source; no explicit seed is accepted by this overload.

Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

Stable laws are characterized most generally through a characteristic function, not an elementary density formula. The α, β, scale and location conventions must match the implementation, especially at α=1; sampling support does not imply every PDF/CDF has a closed form.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real StudentT.CDF(real location, real scale, real freedom, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The degrees of freedom control tail heaviness. With many degrees of freedom the shape approaches a Gaussian; with few, large deviations are much more likely. The scale parameter is not generally the standard deviation.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

StudentT.CDF(0,1,3,0)

Result: 0.5

The center splits the probability in half even though the tails are heavier than Gaussian tails.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real StudentT.InvCDF(real location, real scale, real freedom, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

The degrees of freedom control tail heaviness. With many degrees of freedom the shape approaches a Gaussian; with few, large deviations are much more likely. The scale parameter is not generally the standard deviation.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

Worked example

StudentT.CDF(0,1,3,0)

Result: 0.5

The center splits the probability in half even though the tails are heavier than Gaussian tails.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Probability density . A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

The degrees of freedom control tail heaviness. With many degrees of freedom the shape approaches a Gaussian; with few, large deviations are much more likely. The scale parameter is not generally the standard deviation.

FunctionInfo.Title: Discrete data transform
FunctionInfo.Description:
Complex[] Transform(Complex[] functionPoints, string transformate)
Double[] Transform(Double[] functionPoints, string transformate)

Applies a named transform to an array of equally spaced samples.

Real orthonormal Hartley transform

Arguments / value: Case-sensitive names: FFT, IFFT, DST, IDST, DCT, IDCT, DHT, FHT and IFHT. FHT here means Hilbert transform; DHT means Hartley.

Important: Complex DCT/IDCT/DHT treat the samples as an N-by-2 real array with columns Re and Im, transform BOTH axes with orthonormal scaling, and return N complex coefficients without modifying the input. DCT and IDCT are inverses; DHT is its own inverse. These three complex transforms and real DHT return empty arrays for empty input. Real DHT updates its input in place. Other overload differences: real FFT/IFFT uses Accord DFT and discards the imaginary result; complex FFT/IFFT uses Math.NET defaults and mutates the input array. Several other real transforms also mutate input. Complex FHT/IFHT starts from only the real component. Do not assume every overload is an invertible copy-producing transform.

This operation acts on sampled chart data. A point transformation is not necessarily equivalent to transforming the underlying continuous function, especially after interpolation or numerical differentiation.

Keep an unmodified copy when comparing transformations. The stored sample spacing and chosen chart interval are part of the numerical result.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Transport integral
FunctionInfo.Description:
real TransportJ(integer n, real x)

A Bose-weighted integral used in transport and heat-capacity models.

Definition / convention: Jₙ(x)=∫₀ˣ tⁿ exp(t)/(exp(t)−1)² dt

Arguments / value: Supported integer orders n=2,3,4,5 and real x≥0; other orders return NaN.

Important: This is the unnormalized integral, unlike the separately normalized Debye family.

This thermal transport integral weights modes differently from the Debye integral. The extra factor in the denominator changes the low-temperature and low-argument behavior; the functions are not interchangeable.

Example: TransportJ(2,0) = 0

FunctionInfo.Title: Triangular — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Triangular.CDF(real lower, real upper, real mode, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A bounded piecewise-linear density rising to a mode and then falling to zero.

Definition / convention: f(x)=2(x−lower)/[(upper−lower)(mode−lower)] left of mode; 2(upper−x)/[(upper−lower)(upper−mode)] right of it.

Arguments / value: lower<upper, lower≤mode≤upper; support [lower,upper]. Endpoint modes use one-sided limiting formulas.

Important: The mode need not be the midpoint. Equal lower/upper is a degenerate limit, not the displayed ordinary density. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

The minimum, maximum and mode specify two straight density slopes. The mode is the peak position, not necessarily the midpoint or mean. Endpoint modes are limiting cases of the displayed interior-mode formula.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Distribution model

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Triangular — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Triangular.InvCDF(real lower, real upper, real mode, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A bounded piecewise-linear density rising to a mode and then falling to zero.

Definition / convention: f(x)=2(x−lower)/[(upper−lower)(mode−lower)] left of mode; 2(upper−x)/[(upper−lower)(upper−mode)] right of it.

Arguments / value: lower<upper, lower≤mode≤upper; support [lower,upper]. Endpoint modes use one-sided limiting formulas. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: The mode need not be the midpoint. Equal lower/upper is a degenerate limit, not the displayed ordinary density. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

The minimum, maximum and mode specify two straight density slopes. The mode is the peak position, not necessarily the midpoint or mean. Endpoint modes are limiting cases of the displayed interior-mode formula.

A quantile reverses the CDF question: instead of asking how much probability lies below a value, choose the accumulated probability and obtain its threshold. Use 0.95 for the 95th percentile, not 95.

FunctionInfo.Title: Weibull — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Weibull.CDF(real shape, real scale, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale).

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Shape one gives an exponential waiting-time model. Shapes above one describe increasing hazard, while shapes below one describe decreasing hazard; the scale controls the horizontal unit of the distribution.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Worked example

Weibull.CDF(1,2,2)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

Shape one is exponential with scale two; x=2 is one scale unit.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Weibull — Estimate distribution parameters
FunctionInfo.Description:
Weibull Weibull.Estimate(IEnumerable`1 samples, Random randomSource)

Fits a distribution object to the supplied sample sequence. A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: samples is a finite, nonempty data sequence; randomSource configures subsequent draws, not the fitting data. Use enough nondegenerate observations to estimate the spread.

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. Use positive lifetime observations. Fitting is numerical and can fail for invalid or degenerate samples; it is not a goodness-of-fit test.

Shape one gives an exponential waiting-time model. Shapes above one describe increasing hazard, while shapes below one describe decreasing hazard; the scale controls the horizontal unit of the distribution.

Parameter estimation answers which parameters summarize the observations under this model. It does not establish that the model fits the data; inspect residuals, tail behavior and domain assumptions separately.

Worked example

Weibull.CDF(1,2,2)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

Shape one is exponential with scale two; x=2 is one scale unit.

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale).

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Shape one gives an exponential waiting-time model. Shapes above one describe increasing hazard, while shapes below one describe decreasing hazard; the scale controls the horizontal unit of the distribution.

real Weibull.PDF(real shape, real scale, real x)

Probability density . A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale). Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

Shape one gives an exponential waiting-time model. Shapes above one describe increasing hazard, while shapes below one describe decreasing hazard; the scale controls the horizontal unit of the distribution.

For a short interval of width around , probability is approximately when the density changes slowly there. The approximation improves as the interval shrinks; it is not a probability assigned to the single point .

FunctionInfo.Title: Wishart — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool Wishart.IsValidParameterSet(real degreesOfFreedom, Matrix scale)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A distribution over symmetric positive-definite scatter matrices.

Definition / convention: For integer ν: X=Σ[j=1..ν] zⱼzⱼᵀ with independent zⱼ~Normal(0,scale); E[X]=ν·scale.

Arguments / value: scale is a real d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix; degreesOfFreedom=ν>d−1 gives a nonsingular law.

Important: A sample is a matrix, not an elementwise independent collection of gamma draws. The library’s parameter precheck is not a substitute for matrix positive definiteness. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

For integer degrees of freedom the sample is a sum of outer products of independent Gaussian vectors. This construction explains positive semidefiniteness; sufficient rank and the stated parameter conditions are needed for a nonsingular law.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

FunctionInfo.Title: Radial Zernike polynomial
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ZernikeR(integer n, integer m, real ρ)

The radial factor in Zernike modes on a unit disk, used in optical-aberration analysis.

Definition / convention: Rₙᵐ(ρ)=Σₛ₌₀^((n−m)/2) (−1)ˢ(n−s)!ρ^(n−2s)/[s!((n+m)/2−s)!((n−m)/2−s)!]

Arguments / value: Integers n≥0, 0≤m≤n and 0≤ρ≤1. A nonzero radial polynomial requires n−m even.

Important: No angular sin(mθ)/cos(mθ) factor or unit-RMS optical normalization is included.

Degree, order and evaluation coordinate are separate inputs. Changing a degree chooses another member of the family, not another point on the same curve. The normalization and weighting convention determine how coefficients from different references can be compared.

Example: ZernikeR(2,0,0) = -1

FunctionInfo.Title: Finite Zipf — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Zipf.CDF(real s, integer n, real x)

Returns , the accumulated probability through . A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

The result is a rank between one and a finite maximum. Increasing the exponent concentrates probability toward the first ranks. This finite normalization differs from the infinite zeta distribution.

To find an interval probability, subtract cumulative probabilities at its boundaries. For a continuous law use F(b)−F(a); for an integer-valued law, P(a≤X≤b)=F(b)−F(a−1). The distinction prevents losing the mass at the lower endpoint.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Finite Zipf — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool Zipf.IsValidParameterSet(real s, integer n)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

The result is a rank between one and a finite maximum. Increasing the exponent concentrates probability toward the first ranks. This finite normalization differs from the infinite zeta distribution.

Use this as an early input check, then handle errors from the actual operation. Accepted parameters can include limiting cases with infinite moments or a singular density, so a true result is not a general numerical guarantee.

FunctionInfo.Title: Finite Zipf — Probability mass P(X=k)
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Zipf.PMF(real s, integer n, integer k)

Probability mass . A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n. Evaluate at integer k in the stated support.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. A mass is a point probability between 0 and 1.

The result is a rank between one and a finite maximum. Increasing the exponent concentrates probability toward the first ranks. This finite normalization differs from the infinite zeta distribution.

Add point masses for disjoint allowed outcomes to obtain their combined probability. Unlike a continuous density, this number already refers to an individual outcome, so no bin width is needed.

The result is a rank between one and a finite maximum. Increasing the exponent concentrates probability toward the first ranks. This finite normalization differs from the infinite zeta distribution.

FunctionInfo.Title: Finite Zipf — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
integer Zipf.Sample(Random rnd, real s, integer n)

Returns one random draw. A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Distribution model

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources.

The result is a rank between one and a finite maximum. Increasing the exponent concentrates probability toward the first ranks. This finite normalization differs from the infinite zeta distribution.

A random draw is one simulated outcome, not an expected value. For reproducible experiments supply a seeded generator where the overload permits one; for lazy sample sequences, take a finite number before materializing them.

Distance between adjacent {220} planes of the reference silicon lattice.

Important: The leading underscore is part of the application identifier. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

The symbol in a physical equation denotes a quantity with units; this identifier evaluates to a plain number. Supply the other quantities in the compatible units shown in this entry, because the expression engine does not attach dimensional units or convert them automatically.

FunctionInfo.Title: Absolute value
FunctionInfo.Description:
real abs(real x)

The nonnegative magnitude of a real or complex number.

Definition

Arguments / value: Finite scalar input; usual floating-point NaN/infinity propagation applies.

Important: The abs(complex) overload returns a complex value with zero imaginary part; Magnitude returns a real number.

Absolute value is distance from zero. For real numbers it removes the sign; for complex numbers it combines both coordinates into a nonnegative magnitude.

Magnitude does not retain phase. Two different complex numbers can therefore have the same absolute value, and abs(z) must not be used when the direction of z is important.

Example: abs(-3) = 3

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse cosine
FunctionInfo.Description:
real arccos(real x)

The principal inverse of cosine.

Definition

Arguments / value: Results are in radians where interpreted as angles. Real domain [−1,1], range [0,PI].

An inverse function answers which input produces a given output. When several inputs are possible, this routine chooses one branch; the stated domain and range specify which value you receive.

An inverse is not a reciprocal. For example, arccos(x) finds an angle, whereas 1/cos(x) is secant. For complex inputs, branch choices are part of the definition and ordinary real inverse identities cannot be applied across a cut without care.

Example: arccos(1) = 0

FunctionInfo.Title: Cosine
FunctionInfo.Description:
real cos(real x)

The horizontal coordinate on the unit circle; an even sinusoidal function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. All finite real arguments; real values lie in [−1,1].

Cosine is the horizontal coordinate on the unit circle. It starts at one at zero angle, reaches zero at a quarter-turn and returns to one after 2π radians.

Cosine is even: changing the sign of the angle leaves its value unchanged. Together, sine and cosine resolve a vector into perpendicular components; their squared components sum to one.

Example: cos(0) = 1

Reading sine and cosine

Real-angle illustration at θ=π/4 radians: the radius-one point is (cosθ,sinθ)=(√2/2,√2/2). The blue horizontal and orange vertical projections are signed x and y coordinates; the axes also show their negative directions. Complex inputs are not represented by this circle.

Worked example

cos(60*PI/180)

Result: 0.5

Convert the angle to radians first. This is also the horizontal component of a unit vector inclined at sixty degrees.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Cosecant
FunctionInfo.Description:
real cosec(real x)

The reciprocal of sine.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. Undefined at the zeros of sin(t). Real values are outside (−1,1).

Important: Alias of csc; it uses the same convention.

Cosecant is the reciprocal of the vertical unit-circle coordinate. Its reciprocal interpretation explains the poles at integer multiples of π.

A floating-point value near a pole is not a reliable representation of an infinite mathematical limit. On a plot, keep the branches separated rather than treating a large sampled value as a connection across the singularity.

Example: csc(PI/2) ≈ 1

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real digamma(real x)

The derivative of , widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: Alias of psi with the same convention.

Digamma measures how quickly log-gamma changes. It appears when differentiating gamma-based likelihoods or normalization factors with respect to a shape parameter.

At positive integers it is a harmonic sum minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant. This provides an independent way to check values without differentiating gamma numerically.

FunctionInfo.Title: Drop-wave benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
real dropWave(real x, real y)

A radially symmetric oscillatory optimization surface.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x,y; global minimum −1 at (0,0).

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

The objective oscillates with distance from the origin. Its negative sign means the global minimum is the deepest negative value, not the zero approached in the far field.

Reading the landscape

Concentric rings reflect the dependence on distance from the origin. The y=0 slice shows repeated negative troughs, with the deepest value -1 at the centre. The intervening peaks approach zero, which is not the minimizing value.

Result: -1

At zero radius the numerator is two and the denominator is two, with a minus sign.

FunctionInfo.Title: Error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real erf(real x)

The normalized integral of a Gaussian, continued to an entire complex function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real or complex input; erf(0)=0. For real x, erf(x) lies in [−1,1].

The error function accumulates a Gaussian-shaped curve from zero to its argument. It is odd, equals zero at the origin and approaches ±1 along the real axis.

For a standard normal variable, Φ(x)=(1+erf(x/√2))/2. The scaling by √2 and the shift by one half are essential: erf(x) itself is not the standard normal CDF.

Worked example

erf(0)

Result: 0

The integration interval has zero length.

Worked example

erf(1)

Result: approximately 0.8427007929

This is the accumulated Gaussian integral in the erf convention, not the probability that a standard normal is below one.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential
FunctionInfo.Description:
real exp(real x)

Raises Euler’s number to a real or complex power.

Definition

Arguments / value: Finite real or complex argument; large real parts can overflow or underflow.

The exponential describes growth or decay at a rate proportional to the current value. In A·exp(k·t), a positive k means growth and a negative k means decay; changing A rescales the initial amount.

A real exponential is positive. For imaginary arguments it describes rotation, which connects exponentials to sine and cosine. Very large real parts can overflow floating-point range.

Worked example

exp(0)

Result: 1

Zero elapsed time leaves the initial multiplier unchanged.

Worked example

exp(-1)

Result: approximately 0.3678794412

After one time constant, exponential decay has about 36.8 percent of its initial amount.

FunctionInfo.Title: Factorial
FunctionInfo.Description:
real factorial(real n)

Product of the positive integers up to , with the empty product equal to one.

Definition

Arguments / value: Intended for nonnegative integer n. Returns a floating-point approximation; n≥171, including positive infinity, returns positive infinity immediately because 171! exceeds the finite range of a double.

Important: This loop accepts a real n: fractional n is effectively truncated by the loop and negative n returns 1. It is not Γ(n+1) analytic continuation; use gamma explicitly for that.

Factorial counts the orderings of n distinct objects. At each position there is one fewer choice, giving n·(n−1)·…·1. The empty arrangement explains the convention 0!=1.

This routine is an integer-product helper even though its argument type permits nonintegers. Use the separate gamma function for analytic continuation, and read the implementation warning before supplying fractional or negative inputs.

Worked example

factorial(5)

Result: 120

Five distinct objects have 5·4·3·2·1 possible orders.

FunctionInfo.Title: Bracketed scalar root search
FunctionInfo.Description:
real findRoot(function f, real a, real b)

Attempts to find a zero of the supplied real function within .

Definition / convention: Find x such that f(x)=0.

Arguments / value: Supply a callable f and finite endpoints with a<b that bracket a continuous root.

Important: This convenience wrapper fixes accuracy at 0.01 and maximum iterations at 10,000, catches solver exceptions and returns NaN on failure. Use FunctionRoot methods when you need explicit controls.

A sign-changing bracket for a continuous function guarantees at least one root, but not uniqueness. A pole can also change sign, so continuity across the bracket is essential.

Verify both the reported location and its residual f(x*). A small residual can correspond to a large location error near a flat root; a narrow interval alone can also be misleading near a discontinuity.

Example: findRoot(x => x*x-2,0,2) ≈ 1.414 (within the requested accuracy)

FunctionInfo.Title: Gamma function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real gamma(real x)

The meromorphic extension of the factorial relation to noninteger arguments.

Definition

Arguments / value: Simple poles at 0,−1,−2,…; finite negative nonintegers are defined by continuation. Large magnitudes may overflow.

Important: Γ(n)=(n−1)!, not n!. The complex gamma function is single-valued away from its poles.

Gamma extends the factorial relation beyond whole numbers. The shift matters: , so the continuous counterpart of is , not .

In the integral, controls the behavior near zero and suppresses the far tail. Outside the integral’s convergence region the function is defined by analytic continuation, except at its poles. For large positive arguments, logGamma can avoid forming an overflowing gamma value.

gamma(5)

Result: 24

Apply the recurrence four times: Γ(5)=4·3·2·1·Γ(1), and Γ(1)=1.

Arguments / value: Integers; nonpositive numbers and 1 are not prime.

Primality asks whether there are nontrivial positive divisors. The two public helpers have different output contracts: isPrime is a predicate, while prime is a numeric flag and does not return the n-th prime.

Example: isPrime(13) = true

Mathematical interpretation

FunctionInfo.Title: Symmetry predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool isSymmetric<T>(Matrix M)

Tests equality with the ordinary transpose.

Definition / convention: M=Mᵀ

Arguments / value: A matrix to compare with its transpose.

Important: For complex matrices this is symmetry, not Hermitian symmetry.

Symmetry compares transposed coordinates, without complex conjugation. For complex matrices, a symmetric matrix need not be Hermitian.

Mathematical interpretation

FunctionInfo.Title: Approximate row-unitarity predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
bool isUnitary<T>(Matrix M)

Checks the product with the conjugate transpose against identity.

Definition / convention: M·Mᴴ≈I, using the isIndentity tolerance 1e−10.

Arguments / value: A square matrix satisfying this condition is unitary (orthogonal when real).

Important: The wrapper does not require a square matrix, so rectangular matrices with orthonormal rows can also pass.

For square matrices, unitarity preserves complex inner products. This wrapper checks row orthonormality and does not itself enforce a square shape; rectangular matrices require a more precise interpretation.

FunctionInfo.Title: Kernel or null-space basis
FunctionInfo.Description:
Vector`1[] ker<T>(Matrix M)

Returns basis vectors annihilated by the matrix.

Definition / convention: M·v≈0 for every returned basis vector v.

Arguments / value: Real or complex matrix; returns an array of vectors, possibly empty.

Important: The basis is not unique and numerical rank thresholds affect its dimension.

The kernel contains vectors mapped to zero. A returned basis spans the whole null space, but individual basis vectors are not unique. Verify the residual of A times each basis vector.

FunctionInfo.Title: Least common multiple
FunctionInfo.Description:
real lcm(integer a, integer b)

The smallest positive integer divisible by both positive integer inputs.

Definition / convention: lcm(a,b)=a·b/gcd(a,b).

Arguments / value: Use positive integers. The intermediate integer product can overflow.

Important: The wrapper returns NaN if either argument is zero; it does not implement the conventional zero least-common-multiple value.

A least common multiple gives the first positive coincidence of two integer periods. The product formula is mathematical; intermediate integer arithmetic can overflow before division in this implementation.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

lcm(4,6)

Result: 12

A period-four and a period-six event first coincide again at twelve.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Lower regularized gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real leftRegularizedGamma(real a, real x)

The accumulated lower gamma-integral fraction, also a gamma-distribution tail.

Definition / convention: P(a,x)=∫₀ˣ t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt/Γ(a)

Arguments / value: Use a>0 and x≥0; results then lie in [0,1]. P(a,x)+Q(a,x)=1.

Important: The second argument is the integration limit, not a scale parameter.

The lower regularized gamma function is a fraction of the complete gamma integral. For positive shape and nonnegative x it lies between zero and one. Together with the upper fraction Q it sums to one.

Example: P(1,0)=0 in this convention.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

gammaP(1,1)

Result: approximately 0.6321205588

At shape one the integral is 1−exp(−1).

FunctionInfo.Title: Natural logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ln(real x)

Logarithm to base ; inverse of the real exponential.

Definition

Arguments / value: Finite real domain x>0; x=0 gives −∞. Complex input uses the principal logarithm, with imaginary part given by the principal argument.

A logarithm turns multiplication into addition: for positive real inputs. This is useful for combining likelihoods or working with products too small to represent directly.

The real natural logarithm requires . A complex logarithm also records phase and chooses a branch; adding describes other branches rather than another value returned by the same call.

Worked example

ln(e)

Result: 1

The natural logarithm and exponential undo one another on positive real values.

Computes without requiring a representable unscaled value.

Arguments / value: Real ν≥0 and x>0 in this wrapper; otherwise NaN.

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real logGamma(real x)

Evaluates without first forming a possibly overflowing gamma value.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x>0 only in this wrapper; x≤0 returns NaN.

Important: A complex log-gamma value need not equal the principal logarithm of a separately rounded complex gamma value.

Log-gamma keeps a rapidly growing gamma value in logarithmic form. It is useful in factorial ratios and statistical log-likelihoods, where adding and subtracting log-gamma values can replace products and quotients.

For a positive real argument the result is the natural logarithm of Γ(x). A complex logarithm has a branch convention; it need not agree with taking the principal log of an already rounded gamma result.

Example: logGamma(1) = 0

Worked example

logGamma(5)

Result: approximately 3.1780538303

This is ln(24). Using the direct log-gamma routine becomes more important when Γ(x) itself overflows.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Dense matrix from a rectangular array
FunctionInfo.Description:
Matrix matrix(Complex[,] array)
Matrix matrix(Double[,] array)
Matrix matrix(Int32[,] array)
T matrix(Object[,] array)

Copies a rectangular two-dimensional array into a Math.NET real or complex dense matrix.

Definition / convention: M[row,column] corresponds to array[row,column]; indices start at zero.

Arguments / value: Integer arrays become real matrices; real and complex arrays retain that numerical domain. The dynamic array overload chooses complex if it finds a complex element.

Important: Dynamic elements must be convertible to the chosen scalar type. A matrix is not a jagged array; rows must have consistent lengths.

Rows and columns have different roles: row i and column j select one entry, using zero-based indices. Create a small matrix first and verify its shape before applying an operation to a larger data set.

Arguments / value: Nonnegative dimensions within available memory; library-specific zero-size constraints apply.

Important: For generic numeric matrix creation use T=real (double) or T=complex. The wrapper’s attempted cast for other numeric T can return null; the generic-looking name is not a guarantee of all scalar types.

Arguments / value: i,j are zero-based starting indices; m,n are row/column counts within M.

FunctionInfo.Title: Greatest common divisor
FunctionInfo.Description:
real nwd(integer a, integer b)

The largest positive integer dividing both integer inputs.

Definition / convention: gcd(a,b) divides a and b; gcd(12,18)=6.

Arguments / value: Use positive integers for this implementation.

Important: Alias of gcd; it uses the same convention. The wrapper returns NaN if either input is zero, rather than the common gcd(a,0)=|a| convention; its Euclidean loop does not normalize negative inputs.

Euclid’s reduction replaces a divisibility problem by a smaller remainder problem. Use the positive-integer domain specified by this wrapper; its zero and negative-input behavior is not the general number-theory convention.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

gcd(12,18)

Result: 6

Six is the largest positive integer dividing both values.

FunctionInfo.Title: Interactive desktop plot
FunctionInfo.Description:
void plot(Function f, real XMin, real XMax, real YMin, real YMax, real quality)

Displays a precompiled Function in the renderer selected by its FunctionType.

Arguments / value: Explicit bounds use XMin<XMax and YMin<YMax; quality is multiplied by 100 before being sent to the chart. Default bounds are −5…5 and default quality 0.5 where supplied.

Important: This opens a modal Windows plot dialog; it does not return an image or implement server-side rendering. Browser users should use the Chart screen. Data-series orientation follows the historical AddDataPoints adapters, and mismatched sequence lengths can fail.

A plotted curve or surface is a sampled representation. Insufficient resolution can hide oscillations and discontinuities, and joining samples across a pole can suggest a false continuous curve. Adjust bounds and sampling quality to the feature being investigated.

FunctionInfo.Title: Polygamma of integer order
FunctionInfo.Description:
real polyGamma(integer n, real x)

The -th derivative of the digamma function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0; avoid gamma poles in x. n=1 is trigamma, n=2 tetragamma.

The order counts derivatives of digamma. Order zero is digamma itself; order one is trigamma, the curvature of log-gamma.

Different orders describe different functions, not powers of one function. In particular, the superscript on denotes differentiation, not exponentiation.

Worked example

polyGamma(1,1)

Result: approximately 1.6449340668

Trigamma at one equals the reciprocal-square sum π²/6.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real polyGamma(real x)

The derivative of , widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: The one-argument polyGamma/ψn/ψⁿ names mean order zero, i.e. digamma, not trigamma.

Digamma measures how quickly log-gamma changes. It appears when differentiating gamma-based likelihoods or normalization factors with respect to a shape parameter.

At positive integers it is a harmonic sum minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant. This provides an independent way to check values without differentiating gamma numerically.

Worked example

psi(1)

Result: approximately -0.5772156649

The harmonic sum H₀ is empty, leaving minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Power
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex pow(complex x, complex y)
real pow(real x, real y)

Raises the first argument to the second. The real and complex overloads share this completion signature.

Definition / convention: pow(x,y)=xʸ; for nonzero complex x, exp(y·Log(x)).

Arguments / value: Real negative bases with nonintegral exponents can produce NaN. The complex overload selects a branch, not all possible powers.

A positive real base has an unambiguous real power. A negative base with a noninteger exponent generally requires a complex branch; integer exponents remain repeated multiplication. Use the overload’s domain rather than assuming every real pair produces a finite result.

Example: pow(2,3) = 8

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

pow(2,5)

Result: 32

An integer exponent means five factors of two.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

Raises a square matrix to an integer power using matrix multiplication.

Definition / convention: M⁰=I; M⁻ⁿ=(M⁻¹)ⁿ for n>0.

Arguments / value: Square M; negative n requires invertibility. All signed 32-bit integer exponents are accepted, including -2147483648.

Important: This is not an elementwise power. Large powers can overflow or underflow, and negative powers of ill-conditioned matrices can amplify numerical error.

A matrix power uses matrix multiplication, not elementwise exponentiation. For square matrices the zero power is identity; read the implementation’s restrictions before requesting a negative or noninteger exponent.

FunctionInfo.Title: Numeric primality flag
FunctionInfo.Description:
integer prime(real x)

A numeric wrapper around isPrime, useful in expressions that need a 0/1 indicator.

Definition / convention: prime(x)=1 if the converted integer is prime; otherwise 0.

Arguments / value: The wrapper returns −1 when x<1; otherwise it casts x to a 32-bit integer.

Important: This does not return the x-th prime. Use integral values in the integer range; fractions are truncated.

Primality asks whether there are nontrivial positive divisors. The two public helpers have different output contracts: isPrime is a predicate, while prime is a numeric flag and does not return the n-th prime.

Example: prime(13) = 1

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real psi(real x)

The derivative of , widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Digamma measures how quickly log-gamma changes. It appears when differentiating gamma-based likelihoods or normalization factors with respect to a shape parameter.

At positive integers it is a harmonic sum minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant. This provides an independent way to check values without differentiating gamma numerically.

Worked example

psi(1)

Result: approximately -0.5772156649

The harmonic sum H₀ is empty, leaving minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

FunctionInfo.Title: Uniform random value from zero
FunctionInfo.Description:
real random(integer x)
real random(real x)

Generates a pseudorandom real or integer-valued result according to overload selection.

Definition / convention: Real x: x·U; integer x: an integer from 0 THROUGH x; U∈[0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: Use real x≥0 for [0,x), integer x≥0 for the inclusive integer range. Negative integer x returns NaN. Integer MaxValue cannot safely be used because the implementation adds 1.

Read the typed overload: integer limits use an inclusive integer interval, while real arguments scale a continuous draw. An interval endpoint in an example is not a promise that random sampling will hit it in a finite run.

A complex overload has its own stated geometric convention. Independent real and imaginary draws fill a rectangle, whereas one shared interpolation parameter stays on a line segment; these are different distributions.

Sampling model

FunctionInfo.Title: Upper regularized gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real rightRegularizedGamma(real a, real x)

The remaining upper gamma-integral fraction, also a gamma-distribution tail.

Definition / convention: Q(a,x)=∫ₓ^∞ t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt/Γ(a)

Arguments / value: Use a>0 and x≥0; results then lie in [0,1]. P(a,x)+Q(a,x)=1.

Important: The second argument is the integration limit, not a scale parameter.

This is the upper fraction, not the lower fraction. A dedicated upper-tail evaluation avoids subtracting a CDF already rounded to one when the remaining probability is very small.

Example: Q(1,0)=1 in this convention.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

gammaQ(1,1)

Result: approximately 0.3678794412

At shape one the upper tail equals exp(−1).

FunctionInfo.Title: Exposed pseudorandom generator
FunctionInfo.Description:
Random rnd

The public System.Random instance available to scripts.

Definition / convention: rnd.NextDouble() returns a pseudorandom value in [0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: This is stateful pseudorandomness, not cryptographic randomness. Assigning or seeding rnd does not seed the separate private generator used by random(...).

FunctionInfo.Title: Root by reciprocal exponent
FunctionInfo.Description:
T root(real x, real n)

Computes a power with exponent ; it does not enumerate all roots.

Definition / convention: root(t,n)=pow(t,1/n).

Arguments / value: Use n≠0. Negative real t is promoted to a complex power when its reciprocal exponent is nonintegral. Thus an odd real n does not guarantee the negative real root.

An n-th root solves a power equation; a complex nonzero number has n distinct roots for positive integer n. This helper selects the branch described in the argument guidance, not all roots at once. Use the original convention to decide what negative real inputs mean.

Example: root(8,3) ≈ 2

FunctionInfo.Title: Secant
FunctionInfo.Description:
real sec(real x)

The reciprocal of cosine.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. Undefined at the zeros of cos(t). Real values are outside (−1,1).

Secant is the reciprocal of the horizontal unit-circle coordinate. Where that coordinate vanishes, there is no finite real secant.

A floating-point value near a pole is not a reliable representation of an infinite mathematical limit. On a plot, keep the branches separated rather than treating a large sampled value as a connection across the singularity.

Example: sec(0) = 1

FunctionInfo.Title: Sine
FunctionInfo.Description:
real sin(real x)

The vertical coordinate on the unit circle; models a sinusoidal oscillation.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. All finite real arguments; real values lie in [−1,1].

On a circle of radius one, is the vertical coordinate after rotating through radians. Increasing the angle by a full turn, , returns to the same point; changing its sign reflects the vertical coordinate.

For an oscillation , sets the amplitude, is angular frequency in radians per unit time and is the starting phase. Convert degrees by multiplying by before evaluation.

Example: sin(PI/2) ≈ 1

Reading sine and cosine

Real-angle illustration at θ=π/4 radians: the radius-one point is (cosθ,sinθ)=(√2/2,√2/2). The blue horizontal and orange vertical projections are signed x and y coordinates; the axes also show their negative directions. Complex inputs are not represented by this circle.

Worked example

sin(30*PI/180)

Result: 0.5

Thirty degrees is π/6 radians. Passing 30 without the conversion would ask for the sine of 30 radians, a different angle.

FunctionInfo.Title: Unnormalized cardinal sine
FunctionInfo.Description:
real sinc(real x)

A removable-singularity extension of sine divided by its argument. Useful for oscillatory integrals and wave analysis.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. The value at zero is explicitly supplied, for both real and complex inputs.

Important: This is sin(t)/t, NOT sin(PI·t)/(PI·t).

The ratio has a removable singularity: both numerator and denominator approach zero, but their ratio approaches one. The function supplies that limiting value explicitly, so a graph does not have a hole at the origin.

The nonzero real zeros occur at integer multiples of π. Signal-processing texts often use a normalized sinc whose zeros occur at nonzero integers; that is a different scaling of the argument.

Worked example

sinc(0)

Result: 1

Use the supplied continuous value instead of evaluating 0/0.

Worked example

sinc(PI)

Result: approximately 0

This is the first positive zero. Floating-point evaluation may leave a tiny residual.

FunctionInfo.Title: Six-hump camel benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
real sixHumpCamel(real x, real y)

A two-dimensional polynomial with multiple local minima and two symmetric global minima.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real x,y; global minima are about −1.031628 at (±0.089842,∓0.712656).

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

Several stationary points coexist, including two symmetry-related global minima. A solver returning a stationary point has not necessarily found the best minimum; compare the objective and local curvature.

Reading the landscape

Two symmetry-related global basins are marked. The horizontal slice uses the rounded y-coordinate of the lower basin and passes close to its minimum, near x=0.089842. Other closed contours correspond to higher basins; a stationary point need not be globally best.

Worked example

sixHumpCamel(0.089842,-0.712656)

Result: approximately -1.0316284535

These rounded coordinates lie very close to one global minimum. Negating both coordinates gives the symmetry-related basin with the same objective value; the origin instead has value zero.

Treats the last column of M as the right-hand side and the preceding columns as the coefficient matrix.

Definition / convention: For M=[A|b], returns x solving A·x≈b.

Arguments / value: At least two columns; dimensions/rank must suit the underlying Math.NET solver.

Important: Do not pass just A and expect an implicit right-hand side. Rectangular or ill-conditioned systems follow Math.NET solver behavior.

FunctionInfo.Title: Square root
FunctionInfo.Description:
T sqrt(real x)

Selects the nonnegative real square root, or the principal complex square root.

Definition

Arguments / value: The real-input wrapper promotes negative x to a complex result; its return type is dynamic. Complex input returns the principal root.

A positive real number has two square roots with opposite signs; sqrt selects the nonnegative one. It does not return a pair of roots.

Negative inputs need the complex overload for a complex result. Squaring a principal complex square root recovers its argument, but taking the principal square root of does not always recover .

Example: sqrt(-1) = i

Worked example

sqrt(9)

Result: 3

The other solution of y²=9 is −3; it is not the value selected by sqrt.
