Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. Poles occur where cos(t)=0; for real t these are PI/2+k·PI.

Tangent gives the slope of a line at the specified angle. Near a vertical line, cosine approaches zero and the slope becomes very large.

A floating-point value near a pole is not a reliable representation of an infinite mathematical limit. On a plot, keep the branches separated rather than treating a large sampled value as a connection across the singularity.

Example: tan(PI/4) ≈ 1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Tangent — complex argument
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex tan(complex z)

The ratio of sine to cosine.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. Complex argument z; the formula gives its complex continuation. Reciprocal functions retain poles at zeros of their denominators.

Tangent gives the slope of a line at the specified angle. Near a vertical line, cosine approaches zero and the slope becomes very large.

A floating-point value near a pole is not a reliable representation of an infinite mathematical limit. On a plot, keep the branches separated rather than treating a large sampled value as a connection across the singularity.

Example: tan(PI/4) ≈ 1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Hyperbolic tangent
FunctionInfo.Description:
real tanh(real x)

The ratio of hyperbolic sine to hyperbolic cosine.

Definition

Arguments / value: Angles are measured in radians. For finite real t the mathematical result lies in (−1,1); floating-point saturation can reach an endpoint.

Hyperbolic tangent smoothly compresses the whole real line into the interval between minus one and one. Its slope at zero is one and its tails saturate.

Hyperbolic functions use exponentials, not angles on the unit circle. Their names do not imply periodicity on the real axis.

Example: tanh(0) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

Constructs a real or complex Math.NET column vector from the listed elements.

FunctionInfo.Title: Write text to file
FunctionInfo.Description:
void write(File file, Object o)

Formats o and writes through an existing Computator File wrapper.

Definition / convention: No newline is appended.

Arguments / value: Real/complex numbers and matrices use the application’s display formatting; null is formatted as empty text.

Important: The File wrapper writes in append mode and flushes. The caller still owns its lifetime.

File operations affect external state, unlike a pure mathematical expression. Use a deliberate working directory and a disposable example file when learning. Check the stated append/overwrite and ownership rules; opening a writer is not a numerical calculation.

Formats o and appends it to the current script-output callback.

Important: The executing host must supply an output callback. API/portable hosts impose output limits; output is not a native console requirement.

FunctionInfo.Title: Upper incomplete gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Γ(real a, real x)

The tail of the gamma integral, without division by .

Definition

Arguments / value: Real a>0 and x≥0; other inputs are rejected by this wrapper.

Important: Alias of gamma with the same convention. Do not confuse this with the lower incomplete gamma or the normalized tails gammaP/gammaQ.

The lower limit x removes the beginning of the complete gamma integral, leaving an unnormalized upper tail. Divide by Γ(a) to obtain the regularized upper fraction, or use the dedicated upper-tail routine.

For a=1 the power of t disappears and the remaining integral is exp(−x). This is a convenient independent check of the argument order and upper-tail convention.

Worked example

gamma(1,2)

Result: approximately 0.1353352832

Integrating exp(−t) from two to infinity gives exp(−2).

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Gamma function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real Γ(real x)

The meromorphic extension of the factorial relation to noninteger arguments.

Definition

Arguments / value: Simple poles at 0,−1,−2,…; finite negative nonintegers are defined by continuation. Large magnitudes may overflow.

Important: Alias of gamma with the same convention. Γ(n)=(n−1)!, not n!. The complex gamma function is single-valued away from its poles.

Gamma extends the factorial relation beyond whole numbers. The shift matters: , so the continuous counterpart of is , not .

In the integral, controls the behavior near zero and suppresses the far tail. Outside the integral’s convergence region the function is defined by analytic continuation, except at its poles. For large positive arguments, logGamma can avoid forming an overflowing gamma value.

Worked example

gamma(5)

Result: 24

Apply the recurrence four times: Γ(5)=4·3·2·1·Γ(1), and Γ(1)=1.

Worked example

gamma(0.5)

Result: approximately 1.7724538509

The half-integer value is √π, showing why gamma appears in Gaussian integrals.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Description:

Important: Alias of gamma with the same convention. Γ(n)=(n−1)!, not n!. The complex gamma function is single-valued away from its poles.

FunctionInfo.Title: Beta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real β(real a, real b)

The beta integral; the normalization connecting two gamma factors.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real a>0 and b>0 in this wrapper; symmetric in a and b.

Important: Alias of Beta with the same convention.

The beta integral balances powers of the distances to the two ends of the unit interval. Interchanging a and b reflects t about one half, so the complete beta function is symmetric.

Dividing the integrand by produces a probability density on . The complete special function is a normalization constant, not the Beta distribution object and not a cumulative probability.

Example: Beta(1,1) = 1

Worked example

Beta(2,3)

Result: approximately 0.0833333333

Γ(2)Γ(3)/Γ(5)=1·2/24=1/12.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Lower incomplete beta
FunctionInfo.Description:
real β(real x, real a, real b)

The lower beta integral accumulated up to , without division by the complete beta function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Real 0≤x≤1 and a,b>0; out-of-domain values return NaN. The first argument is the integration limit and the other two are shape parameters.

Important: Alias of Beta with the same convention. The public order is x,a,b; Meta.Numerics receives Beta(a,b,x). This is an unnormalized area: Beta(0,a,b)=0 and Beta(1,a,b)=Beta(a,b). Use BetaNorm for the corresponding cumulative probability.

Incomplete beta stops the beta integral at x rather than at one. It is an accumulated area, not yet a probability until normalized by the complete beta function.

The first argument sets the upper integration limit; a and b determine the shape of the integrand. At x=0 the area is zero, and at x=1 it equals the complete beta function.

Worked example

Beta(0.5,1,1)

Result: 0.5

With both shapes equal to one the integrand is one, so the area from zero to 0.5 is 0.5.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Dirac-delta point helper
FunctionInfo.Description:
real δ(real x)

A pointwise infinity marker used by this application, not an implementation of a Dirac distribution.

Definition / convention: δ(x)=+∞ when x=0; δ(x)=0 otherwise.

Arguments / value: The mathematical Dirac delta is defined by its action on test functions, not as an ordinary sampled function.

Important: Alias of DiracDelta; it uses the same convention. Do not use this helper to expect unit-area plots or correct quadrature of an impulse. Finite-width approximations or analytic integration are needed.

This equation describes the mathematical distribution, NOT a quadrature guarantee for the application’s point helper. Sampling an infinite marker at a grid point does not reproduce its unit-area action. For numerical impulses choose and normalize a finite-width model.

Example: DiracDelta(0) = Infinity

Mathematical interpretation

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Kronecker delta
FunctionInfo.Description:
real δij(real i, real j)

An equality indicator, distinct from the Dirac delta.

Definition / convention: δij=1 when i=j, and 0 otherwise.

Arguments / value: Inputs are compared using exact floating-point equality, even though the usual notation uses integer indices.

Important: Alias of KroneckerDelta; it uses the same convention.

The Kronecker delta selects matching discrete indices, for example diagonal entries of an identity matrix. It is unrelated to an infinitely narrow continuous Dirac impulse.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

KroneckerDelta(2,2)

Result: 1

The indices match exactly.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Hurwitz zeta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ζ(real x, real q)

Shifts the reciprocal-power series away from the positive integers.

Definition / convention: ζ(s,q)=Σₙ₌₀^∞ (n+q)^(−s)

Arguments / value: The argument named x is the exponent s. This real GSL interface requires s>1 and q>0; it is not the full analytic continuation.

Important: Alias of HurwitzZeta with the same convention.

The shift q moves the starting point of the reciprocal-power sum. q=1 recovers Riemann zeta in the convergent half-plane; it is not a second exponent.

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

HurwitzZeta(2,1)

Result: approximately 1.6449340668

At shift one the sum is 1+1/4+1/9+⋯=π²/6.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Dirichlet eta function
FunctionInfo.Description:
real η(real x)

The alternating zeta series, with its removable value supplied at .

Definition / convention: η(s)=Σₙ₌₁^∞ (−1)ⁿ⁻¹/nˢ = (1−2^(1−s))ζ(s)

Arguments / value: Real s; the series converges for s>0, with continuation outside that range.

Important: Alias of DirichletEta with the same convention.

Alternating signs improve convergence compared with the positive zeta series. At s=1 the product representation has a removable cancellation; the limiting value is ln(2).

Mathematical interpretation

Worked example

DirichletEta(1)

Result: approximately 0.6931471806

This is the alternating harmonic sum.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ψ(real x)

The derivative of , widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: Alias of psi with the same convention.

Digamma measures how quickly log-gamma changes. It appears when differentiating gamma-based likelihoods or normalization factors with respect to a shape parameter.

At positive integers it is a harmonic sum minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant. This provides an independent way to check values without differentiating gamma numerically.

Worked example

psi(1)

Result: approximately -0.5772156649

The harmonic sum H₀ is empty, leaving minus the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
complex ψ(complex z)

The derivative of , widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: Alias of psi with the same convention.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Polygamma of integer order
FunctionInfo.Description:
real ψn(integer n, real x)

The -th derivative of the digamma function.

Definition

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0; avoid gamma poles in x. n=1 is trigamma, n=2 tetragamma.

Important: Alias of polyGamma with the same convention.

The order counts derivatives of digamma. Order zero is digamma itself; order one is trigamma, the curvature of log-gamma.

Different orders describe different functions, not powers of one function. In particular, the superscript on denotes differentiation, not exponentiation.

Worked example

polyGamma(1,1)

Result: approximately 1.6449340668

Trigamma at one equals the reciprocal-square sum π²/6.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov
